lessons.title: What a Computer Network Is: Hosts, Links, Packets and the Internet
lessons.content:
Imagine you send a voice message on WhatsApp from Dhaka to your cousin in Sylhet. You press the button, speak for five seconds, let go, and a moment later her phone buzzes. Between your phone and hers there were radio waves, a cell tower, kilometres of fiber cable, maybe a dozen big boxes called routers, a data center that might be in another country, and then the same path in reverse. Nobody planned that exact path for you. It just worked, in less than a second. This course is about how that magic actually works, piece by piece.

What a computer network is: A computer network is a set of devices that can send data to each other over some kind of connection. The devices that run our apps, like phones, laptops, smart TVs and servers, are called hosts or end systems. The connections between them are called communication links: copper cable, fiber optic cable, radio (Wi-Fi, 4G) or satellite. In between the hosts sit packet switches, mainly routers and link-layer switches, whose job is to pass data along towards its destination. That is the whole cast: hosts at the edge, links to carry bits, and switches in the middle.

The problem networks solve: Before networks, if a bank branch in Chattogram wanted to share records with the head office in Motijheel, someone carried paper, or later a floppy disk, by bus. Computers were islands. The first step was to connect two computers with one wire. But a wire between every pair of computers does not scale: with n computers you need n(n-1)/2 wires, so 1,000 computers would need 499,500 wires. The solution is sharing: a few links and switches carry traffic for many users at once. Data Communication taught you how bits travel on one link; this course is about how millions of links work together.

Packets, the key idea: Hosts do not send a big file in one piece. They cut the data into small chunks called packets, each with a header that says where it is going, like the address on an envelope. If you send a 3 MB photo, it may become about 2,000 packets of 1,500 bytes each. Each packet travels hop by hop through routers. A router receives a whole packet, looks at the destination address, and sends it out of the right link. This is called store-and-forward packet switching. Because packets from many users mix on the same links, the links stay busy and no single user hogs a reserved line.

A worked number: A packet of L bits pushed onto a link of rate R bits per second takes L/R seconds just to get onto the wire. For L = 12,000 bits (1,500 bytes) and R = 100 Mbps, that is 12,000 / 100,000,000 = 0.00012 s, or 0.12 ms. If the path has 3 links of the same rate and every router must receive the whole packet before forwarding, the packet needs 3 x 0.12 = 0.36 ms of pushing time, ignoring other delays. We will study all the delays carefully in the next lesson.

What a protocol is: When two people meet, there are rules: you say salam, the other replies, then you talk, and you say goodbye before leaving. If one person suddenly starts shouting numbers, the other is confused. Computers need the same kind of rules, only much stricter. A protocol defines the format of the messages, the order in which they are exchanged, and the actions taken when a message is sent, received, or lost. Examples you will meet: HTTP for the web, SMTP for email, DNS for names, TCP and UDP for delivery between programs, IP for moving packets across the Internet, Ethernet and Wi-Fi for single links.

Who writes the rules: Internet standards are developed by the IETF, the Internet Engineering Task Force. Its documents are called RFCs, Requests for Comments. For example, the original TCP is RFC 793 and the original IP is RFC 791. Link technologies like Ethernet (IEEE 802.3) and Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11) are standardized by the IEEE. Because these documents are public, a phone made in China, a router made in the USA and a server run in Bangladesh can all talk to each other. Standards are what make the Internet one network instead of many incompatible ones.

The nuts-and-bolts view: One way to describe the Internet is by its parts: billions of hosts, connected by links and packet switches, organized into networks owned by Internet Service Providers (ISPs), all running the TCP/IP protocols. In this view the Internet is a giant machine made of hardware and software. You can point at a router, a cable, a server rack. This is how a network engineer at an ISP thinks every day while fixing cables and configuring routers.

The services view: The other way to describe the Internet is by what it offers to applications. The Internet is an infrastructure that provides services to distributed applications, programs running on many hosts that exchange data. Facebook, bKash, YouTube, online exams and multiplayer games are all distributed applications. The Internet gives them a programming interface, called the socket interface, through which a program can say: please deliver these bytes to that program on that host. A developer does not care which cables are used, just like you do not care which road a courier van takes, as long as the parcel arrives.

Network of networks: No single company owns the Internet. Your home Wi-Fi is a small network. It connects to a local ISP, perhaps a broadband company in your area. That ISP connects to a bigger national ISP. National ISPs connect to international gateways and to global transit providers, called tier-1 ISPs, which connect to each other. So the Internet is literally a network of networks, glued together by business agreements. A smaller ISP pays a bigger one (its provider) for transit, while two similar ISPs may agree to exchange traffic for free, which is called peering.

Internet exchange points: If two ISPs in Dhaka want to exchange local traffic, sending it to Singapore and back would be slow and costly. So they meet at an Internet Exchange Point (IXP), a building with switches where many networks connect and peer. Bangladesh has BDIX, which lets local ISPs exchange traffic inside the country. That is why some local servers and cache servers feel very fast on a home connection: the traffic never leaves Bangladesh. Big content companies also run their own networks and place servers close to users, which we will see when we discuss CDNs.

How Bangladesh connects to the world: International traffic leaves Bangladesh mostly through submarine cables landing at Cox's Bazar and Kuakata (SEA-ME-WE 4 and SEA-ME-WE 5), plus terrestrial cables through neighbouring countries. Inside the country, fiber networks carry traffic between cities. When you open a website hosted in the USA, your packets travel this long chain: your device, your ISP, a national backbone, an international gateway, a submarine cable, foreign ISPs, and finally the server. Every hop runs the same basic protocols, which is why it works at all.

LAN, MAN and WAN in one line each: A LAN (local area network) covers a home, office or campus, typically with Ethernet and Wi-Fi. A MAN covers a city, such as a cable operator's network. A WAN covers countries or continents, such as an ISP backbone. You met these and the topologies (bus, star, ring, mesh) in Data Communication, so we only use them as names here.

Circuit switching versus packet switching in one breath: The old telephone network reserved a circuit, a fixed share of every link, for the whole call. Even when you are silent, the reserved capacity is wasted. The Internet uses packet switching, where links are shared on demand. Suppose a 1 Mbps link and users who need 100 kbps but are active only 10% of the time. Circuit switching can support only 10 users. With packet switching, 35 users can share it, and the chance that more than 10 are active at the same moment is less than 0.0004. That statistical sharing is why the Internet is cheap and efficient.

Real life example 1, ordering on Daraz: You tap Place Order. Your phone builds an HTTP request, the request rides inside a TCP segment, which rides inside an IP packet, which rides inside a Wi-Fi frame. The Wi-Fi router passes it to your ISP, which forwards it across several routers to Daraz's servers. The server replies with an order confirmation that comes back as packets, possibly along a different path. Every layer did one small job, and all of them together made a single tap work.

Real life example 2, a cricket live stream: During a Bangladesh vs India match, millions of people watch the same stream. If every viewer pulled the video from one server in another country, that server and the international cables would choke. Instead, streaming services keep copies on servers inside or near Bangladesh, often reachable over BDIX or inside the ISP itself. Your app picks a quality that fits your speed and keeps adjusting. Topics like CDNs, adaptive streaming and congestion control all show up in this one everyday scene.

The course map: We go top-down. First the application layer: HTTP, email, DNS, P2P, streaming and socket programming, because that is what you use every day. Then the transport layer: UDP, reliable data transfer, TCP and congestion control. Then the network layer: routers, IPv4, addressing and subnetting, DHCP, NAT, ICMP, IPv6 and routing algorithms like Dijkstra and Bellman-Ford, plus OSPF and BGP. Then the link layer: MAC addresses, ARP, Ethernet switches and VLANs. Finally wireless networks and network security, ending with a full walk-through of what happens when you open a web page.

How to study networks: Networks are best learned by watching real packets. On any computer you can run ping and traceroute (tracert on Windows) to see delays and the routers on a path. Later you may install Wireshark to look inside packets. You will also do many small calculations: delays, round trip times, subnet ranges, routing tables. Do them on paper with tiny numbers until the pattern is obvious.

Common mistakes: Thinking the Internet and the Web are the same. The Web is one application (HTTP and browsers) running on top of the Internet; email, WhatsApp and online games are other applications. Thinking a router and a switch are the same: a router forwards using IP addresses between networks, a switch forwards using MAC addresses inside one LAN. Thinking data travels as one big piece: it travels as packets. And thinking someone controls the whole Internet: it is many independent networks cooperating.

What exams ask: Define a network, host, link, router and protocol. Describe the Internet from the nuts-and-bolts and service views. Explain the ISP hierarchy, peering and IXPs. Compare circuit and packet switching with a numeric example. Compute L/R for a packet on a link. Short notes on RFC, IETF and network of networks often appear too.

Recap: A network is hosts plus links plus packet switches running protocols. Data moves as packets with headers, forwarded store-and-forward by routers. Protocols fix message format, order and actions. The Internet is a network of networks held together by ISPs, peering and IXPs like BDIX, and it offers a socket interface to applications. Next we measure how fast and how well this machine works: delay, loss and throughput.
key_points: A network has hosts (end systems), communication links and packet switches (routers and switches).
Data is split into packets with headers and forwarded hop by hop using store-and-forward.
A protocol defines message format, message order and the actions taken on send, receive or loss.
Internet standards are written by the IETF as RFCs; Ethernet and Wi-Fi are IEEE standards.
The Internet can be seen as nuts-and-bolts (hardware and software) or as a service to distributed applications.
The Internet is a network of networks: access ISPs, national ISPs, tier-1 ISPs, peering and IXPs such as BDIX.
Packet switching shares links statistically and supports more users than circuit switching for bursty traffic.
The course goes top-down: application, transport, network, link, wireless and security.
lessons.tip: Keep a small notebook page called 'my path to the Internet' and fill it in as the course goes: your device, your Wi-Fi, your ISP, the cables, the protocols. Every new lesson adds one line to it.
lessons.task: Open a terminal or command prompt and run 'ping google.com' and then 'tracert google.com' (Windows) or 'traceroute google.com' (Mac/Linux). Count how many routers appear and note the time to the first and last hop.

quiz.q: What does a protocol define?
options: The format and order of messages and the actions taken
quiz.explain: A protocol fixes message format, the order of exchange and the actions on sending, receiving or loss.

What is BDIX?
options: An Internet Exchange Point where Bangladeshi networks exchange local traffic
quiz.explain: BDIX is an IXP where local ISPs peer so local traffic stays inside Bangladesh.

quiz.q: Which organization publishes Internet standards as RFCs?
quiz.explain: The IETF writes Internet standards, published as RFCs.

quiz.q: Why can packet switching support more users than circuit switching on the same link?
options: Users are not all active at the same time, so capacity is shared on demand
quiz.explain: Bursty users rarely transmit together, so statistical sharing serves many more of them.

lessons.title: Network Edge, Core and Performance: Delay, Loss and Throughput
lessons.content:
Think of a parcel going from a shop in Bogura to your home in Dhaka by courier. First a van picks it up from the shop. That first short trip is the edge. Then it goes onto a highway with trucks and sorting hubs. That is the core. Along the way it waits at hubs, gets loaded onto trucks, drives along roads, and sometimes, sadly, gets lost. The Internet works the same way, and in this lesson we learn to measure exactly how long a packet waits, travels and gets lost.

The network edge: The edge is where users live: phones, laptops, home routers, office PCs, and also the servers in data centers. Hosts are often split into clients, which ask for things, and servers, which answer. Your browser is a client; the Google server is a server. Most big servers today sit in huge data centers with hundreds of thousands of machines. Whatever their size, they are still end systems at the edge of the network.

Access networks, the first link: An access network connects a host to its first router, called the edge router. At home in Bangladesh you might use FTTH (fiber to the home), where a fiber reaches the building and is shared using a passive optical splitter. Older connections used DSL over the telephone wire or cable internet over the TV coaxial cable; those were covered in Data Communication, so we only name them. Many homes use local Ethernet broadband where a cable runs from a building switch to your flat. On the move, your phone uses 4G or 5G mobile access through a base station. Inside the home or office, Ethernet cables and Wi-Fi connect devices to the home router.

The network core: The core is the mesh of routers and high-capacity links that connect access networks. Its main tool is packet switching: messages are cut into packets, and each router stores a whole packet, then forwards it. Routers do two jobs. Forwarding is the local action of moving a packet from an input link to the correct output link, using a forwarding table. Routing is the network-wide process of deciding the paths and filling those tables. We will spend several lessons on each. For now, remember that a packet experiences delay at every router it crosses.

The four delays: At each hop a packet suffers four kinds of delay. Processing delay is the time to read the header, check for bit errors and decide the output link, usually microseconds. Queuing delay is the time spent waiting in the output buffer behind other packets; it can be zero or many milliseconds depending on traffic. Transmission delay is the time to push all the bits of the packet onto the link: L/R, where L is packet length in bits and R is link rate in bits per second. Propagation delay is the time for one bit to travel along the wire: d/s, where d is the length of the link and s is the propagation speed, about 2 x 10^8 m/s in copper or fiber. The total nodal delay is d_proc + d_queue + d_trans + d_prop.

Transmission versus propagation, the toll plaza story: Imagine ten cars driving together as a caravan on a highway. At a toll booth, each car takes 12 seconds to be served. Pushing all ten cars through the booth takes 120 seconds; that is like transmission delay, which depends on how many cars (bits) and how fast the booth works (link rate). Then the cars drive 100 km to the next booth at 100 km/h, taking one hour; that is propagation delay, which depends only on distance and speed. Students often mix these up. Transmission delay has nothing to do with distance; propagation delay has nothing to do with packet size.

Worked example 1: A 1,500-byte packet goes over a 10 Mbps link that is 2,000 km long. L = 1,500 x 8 = 12,000 bits. Transmission delay = 12,000 / 10,000,000 = 0.0012 s = 1.2 ms. Propagation delay = 2,000,000 m / (2 x 10^8 m/s) = 0.01 s = 10 ms. Here propagation dominates. Change the link to 100 m of cable inside a building: propagation becomes 0.5 microseconds, and transmission (still 1.2 ms) dominates. Which one matters depends on the situation, so always compute both.

Worked example 2, end-to-end: Suppose a path has N links, all with rate R, and no queuing. Sending one packet of L bits takes N x L/R of transmission time, plus propagation on each link. Sending P packets back to back through N links takes (N + P - 1) x L/R, because once the pipeline is full, one packet leaves the last link every L/R seconds. For N = 3, P = 4, L/R = 1 ms: (3 + 4 - 1) x 1 = 6 ms. Draw a little timeline with the three links to convince yourself.

Queuing delay and traffic intensity: Let a be the average arrival rate of packets per second at a router output, each of L bits, and R the output link rate. Traffic intensity is La/R. If La/R is greater than 1, bits arrive faster than they can leave, and the queue grows without limit; the golden rule is to design so that La/R stays below 1. When La/R is close to 0, queuing delay is tiny. As La/R approaches 1, average queuing delay shoots up very fast, not slowly. This is why a road that is 90% full feels fine but 98% full is a traffic jam. Example: L = 1,000 bits, a = 900 packets/s, R = 1 Mbps gives La/R = 900,000 / 1,000,000 = 0.9, which is already risky.

Packet loss: Router buffers are finite. When a packet arrives and the buffer is full, the router drops it. That packet is lost. The sender may retransmit it later (TCP does), or the application may simply live with the gap (a video call might show a small glitch). Loss rises sharply as traffic intensity nears 1. So the performance of a network is not only how fast, but also how often packets disappear.

Throughput: Throughput is the rate at which the receiver actually gets bits, in bits per second. Instantaneous throughput is the rate at one moment; average throughput is total bits divided by total time. If a 32 Mbit file takes 4 seconds, average throughput is 8 Mbps. Throughput is different from delay: a pipe can be wide (high throughput) but long (high delay), like a satellite link.

The bottleneck link: For a path of links with rates R1, R2, ..., the end-to-end throughput is roughly the minimum of them, min(R1, R2, ...). If a server has a 100 Mbps link, the core has 10 Gbps links, and your home connection is 20 Mbps, your download cannot exceed 20 Mbps. Worked: a 40 MB file is 320 Mbit; at 20 Mbps it takes 16 seconds at best. If ten users share one 50 Mbps core link equally, each gets 5 Mbps from that link, and if 5 Mbps is below their access rates, the shared core link becomes the bottleneck instead.

Round trip time: RTT is the time for a small packet to go from client to server and back. ping measures it. RTT includes propagation both ways, plus transmission, processing and queuing at each hop. From Dhaka, a server inside Bangladesh may show an RTT of a few milliseconds, a server in Singapore a few tens of milliseconds, and a server in the USA often over 200 ms. Many later formulas, such as HTTP response time and TCP throughput, are written in RTTs.

Traceroute, seeing the delays: traceroute sends packets with a small time-to-live value: first 1, then 2, then 3. Each router reduces the value by one, and when it hits zero, the router drops the packet and sends back an error message. So the first router reveals itself, then the second, and so on. traceroute sends three probes for each hop and prints three times. You often see times jump when a packet crosses a submarine cable. Sometimes a later hop shows a smaller time than an earlier one, because each probe sees a different queue at that moment.

Putting the four together, a worked hop: A router needs 20 microseconds to process a packet, the packet waits behind 3 others of the same size, each 1,000 bytes, on a 10 Mbps output link 500 km long. Transmission of one packet = 8,000 / 10,000,000 = 0.8 ms. Queuing = 3 x 0.8 = 2.4 ms. Propagation = 500,000 / (2 x 10^8) = 2.5 ms. Total nodal delay = 0.02 + 2.4 + 0.8 + 2.5 = 5.72 ms. Notice how waiting in line cost almost as much as the travel itself.

Real life example 1, morning vs night speed: Many students in Dhaka notice that the same broadband feels fast at 7 am and slow at 10 pm. The access link rate did not change. What changed is traffic intensity: at night everyone is streaming, so routers at the ISP and on international links have longer queues, causing higher queuing delay and some loss. Speed tests at both times show lower throughput and higher ping at night. That is La/R creeping toward 1.

Real life example 2, video call to abroad: A student in Rajshahi calls a relative in London on Messenger. Even with a good connection, voice has a slight lag. Most of it is propagation and processing over about 8,000 km plus routing detours: even at 2 x 10^8 m/s, 8,000 km takes 40 ms one way, and real paths are longer. No amount of bandwidth removes propagation delay, because it is set by distance and the speed of light in the medium.

Delay-bandwidth product in one line: The number of bits that fit in a link at once equals R x d_prop. For a 100 Mbps link with 10 ms propagation, that is 1,000,000 bits in flight. You saw this as the bandwidth-delay product in Data Communication; it will return when we discuss why TCP needs large windows.

Common mistakes: Using bytes where bits are needed; always multiply bytes by 8. Mixing up Mbps (megabits) and MBps (megabytes). Adding transmission delay only once for a multi-hop path, when store-and-forward means it is paid on every link. Thinking more bandwidth reduces propagation delay. Forgetting that traffic intensity above 1 means infinite queue in theory, not just big.

What exams ask: Define and compute the four delays. Compare transmission and propagation with the caravan analogy. Compute end-to-end delay for N links and P packets. Compute traffic intensity and comment on queuing. Find throughput and bottleneck for given link rates. Explain how traceroute works. List access network technologies.

Recap: The edge holds hosts and access networks such as FTTH, Ethernet, Wi-Fi and 4G/5G. The core is routers doing store-and-forward packet switching. Each hop adds processing, queuing, transmission (L/R) and propagation (d/s) delay. Queuing and loss depend on traffic intensity La/R. Throughput is limited by the bottleneck link. With these numbers in hand, we can now look at how the work is divided into layers.
key_points: The edge has hosts and access networks (FTTH, Ethernet, DSL, cable, Wi-Fi, 4G/5G); the core has routers.
Nodal delay = processing + queuing + transmission + propagation.
Transmission delay = L/R depends on packet size and link rate; propagation delay = d/s depends on distance.
N store-and-forward links and P packets take (N + P - 1) x L/R of transmission time.
Traffic intensity La/R must stay below 1; queuing delay grows sharply as it approaches 1.
Full buffers cause packet loss.
End-to-end throughput is about the minimum link rate on the path, the bottleneck.
traceroute uses increasing TTL values to reveal each router and its RTT.
lessons.tip: Write every delay problem as a small table: L, R, d, s, then L/R and d/s with units. Converting bytes to bits and km to m first prevents half of all mistakes.
lessons.task: Run a speed test on your phone or computer in the morning and again late at night. Note download speed and ping both times, and explain the difference using traffic intensity and queuing delay.

Which delay depends on the physical length of the link?
quiz.explain: Propagation delay is d/s, distance divided by signal speed.

quiz.q: If traffic intensity La/R is greater than 1, what happens?
quiz.explain: Bits arrive faster than they can leave, so the queue keeps growing.

quiz.q: Links on a path are 100 Mbps, 1 Gbps and 20 Mbps. What is the end-to-end throughput about?
quiz.explain: Throughput is limited by the bottleneck, the slowest link.

lessons.title: Layers and Encapsulation: How the Work of the Internet Is Divided
lessons.content:
Think about how you send Eid gifts to a relative in Khulna through a courier company. You pack the gift and write a note. The courier counter staff put it in their own bag with a tracking label. The bag goes into a sack for Khulna. The sack goes onto a truck. At the Khulna hub, the sack is opened, the bag is sorted, the label is read, and finally your relative opens the box and reads your note. Each person only does one job and only reads the wrapping meant for them. Networks are built exactly like this, and the idea is called layering.

Why layers at all: A network has to do a huge list of jobs: turn bits into signals, send frames on one link, find a path across the world, make delivery reliable, give data to the right program, and make the data meaningful to the app. If one giant program did all of that, changing anything, like moving from Ethernet to Wi-Fi, would mean rewriting everything. Layering splits the problem into a stack of layers. Each layer offers a service to the layer above, using only the service of the layer below. As long as the service stays the same, a layer's inside can be changed freely. Wi-Fi replaced cables in many homes, yet your browser did not change at all.

The five-layer Internet stack: The Internet uses five layers, from top to bottom. Application layer: where network applications and their protocols live, such as HTTP, SMTP, DNS. Transport layer: moves application messages between processes on two hosts, using TCP or UDP. Network layer: moves datagrams from source host to destination host across many routers, using IP and routing protocols. Link layer: moves frames across one single link, from one node to the next, such as Ethernet or Wi-Fi. Physical layer: moves the individual bits on the wire or through the air. A memory trick: All People Need Lots of Pizza, from application down to physical.

The OSI model, a quick recap: In Data Communication you met the 7-layer OSI model from ISO: application, presentation, session, transport, network, data link, physical. The Internet stack merges presentation (data format, encryption, compression) and session (checkpoints, synchronization) into the application layer. If an app needs those services, the app itself or a library provides them. So in exams you may be asked to map the two: OSI's top three layers equal the Internet's application layer, and the bottom four map one to one.

What each layer calls its packet: The data unit has a different name at each layer, and examiners love these names. At the application layer it is a message. At the transport layer it is a segment (TCP) or sometimes a datagram (UDP). At the network layer it is a datagram, also commonly called a packet. At the link layer it is a frame. At the physical layer we just speak of bits. Using the right name tells your teacher which layer you are thinking about.

Encapsulation step by step: Suppose your browser wants to send the message GET /index.html to a server. The application layer hands the message M down. The transport layer adds its header Ht, which contains port numbers and, for TCP, sequence numbers. Now we have a segment: Ht + M. The network layer adds Hn, which has source and destination IP addresses, giving a datagram: Hn + Ht + M. The link layer adds Hl, with MAC addresses, and usually a trailer for error detection, giving a frame: Hl + Hn + Ht + M + trailer. The physical layer sends these as bits. At the receiver the reverse happens: each layer removes its own header, reads it, and passes the rest up. This removal is called decapsulation.

A worked size example: An app sends a 1,000-byte message. TCP adds a 20-byte header: 1,020 bytes. IPv4 adds a 20-byte header: 1,040 bytes. Ethernet adds a 14-byte header and a 4-byte trailer: 1,058 bytes. So 1,000 useful bytes needed 1,058 bytes on the wire, and efficiency is 1,000 / 1,058, about 94.5%. With a 100-byte message the same headers give 100 / 158, about 63%. This is why very tiny packets waste a lot of capacity, and why protocols try not to send many tiny packets.

Peer-to-peer talk between layers: Although data moves down and up the stack physically, each layer logically talks to the same layer on the other side. The transport layer on your laptop puts a sequence number in its header, and only the transport layer on the server reads it. Routers in the middle never look at it. That is why we say each layer has a peer, and each protocol is a conversation between peers at one layer. It is like the courier's tracking label: only courier staff read it; your relative ignores it.

Where each device works: A host implements all five layers, because it runs apps. A router works up to the network layer: it receives a frame, removes the link header, looks at the IP header, chooses an output, wraps the datagram in a new frame for the next link, and sends it. It does not look at TCP or HTTP, at least not for normal forwarding. A link-layer switch works up to the link layer: it reads MAC addresses only. A hub or repeater works only at the physical layer, copying bits. So the IP header survives end to end, but the link header is replaced at every hop.

Addresses at each layer: Each layer has its own way of naming things. The link layer uses 48-bit MAC addresses, like 3C:22:FB:10:7A:01, burned into the network card and meaningful only on one local link. The network layer uses IP addresses, such as 103.4.145.2 for IPv4, which identify a host's interface across the whole Internet. The transport layer uses 16-bit port numbers, like 443 for HTTPS, to identify which process on the host. The application layer uses names people like, such as a domain name like www.example.com or an email address. Translating between these levels is the job of protocols like DNS (names to IP) and ARP (IP to MAC), which we will study.

Service and interface: Each layer offers a service, such as reliable byte delivery (TCP) or best-effort datagram delivery (IP). The point where an upper layer uses a lower layer's service is called an interface. The socket is the interface between application and transport, and it is the only interface most programmers ever touch. Under the socket, the operating system kernel implements transport and network layers, and the network card with its driver handles link and physical. So layers map nicely onto real software and hardware: apps in user space, TCP/IP in the kernel, link and physical in the card.

Disadvantages of layering: Layering is not free. Some functions get duplicated; for example, error checking is done at the link layer with CRC and again at the transport layer with a checksum. Sometimes one layer needs information hidden in another; for instance, a video app might want to know the current Wi-Fi signal strength, which strict layering hides. And headers add overhead, as in our size example. Still, the benefits of modular design are so large that every real network uses layers.

The hourglass shape: People draw the Internet stack like an hourglass. At the top there are thousands of applications. At the bottom there are many link technologies: Ethernet, Wi-Fi, 4G, 5G, fiber, satellite. In the narrow waist there is exactly one network protocol: IP. Everything runs over IP, and IP runs over everything. This narrow waist is the reason a new app can work on any network, and a new link technology can carry every existing app, as long as both speak IP.

A tiny pseudo-code view of layers: You can imagine each layer as a function that wraps the data and calls the one below. send_app(msg) calls send_transport(port_hdr + msg). send_transport calls send_network(ip_hdr + segment). send_network calls send_link(mac_hdr + datagram + crc). On the receiving side, recv_link checks the CRC, strips mac_hdr and calls recv_network, which checks the destination IP, strips ip_hdr and calls recv_transport, which looks at the port to find the right program and hands it msg. Each function knows only its own header. That is the whole idea of layering in four lines, and it is literally how network code inside an operating system is organized.

Who standardizes which layer: Application, transport and network protocols of the Internet are standardized by the IETF in RFCs. Link and physical standards come mostly from the IEEE (802.3 Ethernet, 802.11 Wi-Fi) and, for mobile networks, from 3GPP (4G LTE, 5G). Web formats like HTML are maintained by other bodies. Knowing who owns which layer helps you find the right documents later.

Real life example 1, opening Prothom Alo on Wi-Fi: Your browser creates an HTTP request, a message. TCP adds ports 52000 to 443 and sequence numbers, a segment. IP adds your address and the server's address, a datagram. Wi-Fi adds MAC addresses of your phone and the home router, a frame, sent over radio as bits. The home router strips the Wi-Fi frame, reads the IP header, puts the datagram in a new frame for the ISP's link, and so on. At the far end, the server's layers peel the wrappers off in reverse, and the web server program receives the clean HTTP request.

Real life example 2, a bKash payment over 4G: The bKash app sends an encrypted message over TLS, which runs above TCP. Underneath, the 4G link layer carries the IP datagram from your phone to the base station, then the mobile operator's core network forwards it as IP to the bKash servers. The radio part was completely different from Wi-Fi, yet the app, TLS, TCP and IP layers were identical. That independence is exactly what layering promised.

Common mistakes: Saying a router reads TCP ports during normal forwarding; it uses the IP header. Saying the MAC address stays the same from source to destination; it changes every hop, while the IP addresses stay the same (ignoring NAT, which we will meet later). Mixing up segment, datagram and frame. Forgetting the link-layer trailer. Thinking OSI is what the Internet actually runs; the Internet runs TCP/IP, while OSI is mostly a teaching and reference model.

What exams ask: Draw the five-layer stack and list each layer's job and an example protocol. Map OSI to TCP/IP. Explain encapsulation with a labelled diagram. Name the PDU at each layer. State which layers a host, router, switch and hub implement. Compute overhead or efficiency for given header sizes. List the advantages and disadvantages of layering.

Recap: Layering divides networking into application, transport, network, link and physical layers. Each layer serves the one above and uses the one below. Going down, each layer adds a header (encapsulation); going up, each removes its own (decapsulation). Names change: message, segment, datagram, frame, bits. Hosts run all layers, routers up to network, switches up to link. IP is the narrow waist of the hourglass. Next we climb to the top layer and see how applications are organized.
key_points: Layering splits networking into layers; each serves the one above using the one below.
Internet stack: application, transport, network, link, physical.
OSI's application, presentation and session map to the Internet's application layer.
Data units: message, segment, datagram (packet), frame, bits.
Encapsulation adds a header at each layer going down; decapsulation removes them going up.
Hosts implement all five layers, routers up to network, switches up to link, hubs only physical.
Addresses: MAC at link, IP at network, port at transport, names at application.
IP is the narrow waist: every app runs over IP and IP runs over every link.
lessons.tip: Draw the encapsulation picture with coloured pens once: a small M in the middle, then boxes for Ht, Hn and Hl wrapped around it. Redraw it from memory before every exam; it answers half the layer questions.

quiz.explain: The network layer carries datagrams, also called packets.

quiz.q: Up to which layer does a router normally process a packet?
quiz.explain: A router reads the IP header (network layer) to forward the datagram.

quiz.q: Which OSI layers are merged into the Internet's application layer?
quiz.explain: OSI's presentation and session functions are left to the application in TCP/IP.

options: The MAC address in the frame
quiz.explain: Each link gets a new frame with new MAC addresses; IP addresses stay the same.

lessons.title: Application Layer Principles: Client-Server, P2P, Sockets and Ports
lessons.content:
Imagine a big tea stall at Nilkhet. Customers come and ask for tea; the stall owner is always there, always at the same spot, ready to serve. That is one way to organize things. Now imagine a group of friends in a hostel sharing notes before exams: everyone has some pages, everyone asks others for missing pages, and everyone gives pages to others. There is no boss. These two pictures, the tea stall and the hostel, are the two main ways network applications are organized: client-server and peer-to-peer.

What a network application is: A network application is a set of programs running on different end systems that talk to each other over the network. The web is a browser on your phone and a web server program in a data center. WhatsApp is the app on your phone, the app on your friend's phone and WhatsApp's servers. The key point is that you only write programs for the end systems. You never write code for routers. Routers do not run applications, they only forward packets. This made the Internet a playground: anyone with a laptop can create a new application without asking any ISP for permission.

Client-server architecture: In client-server, there is an always-on host called the server, with a fixed, well-known IP address, that serves requests from many clients. Clients may be on and off, may change IP addresses, and do not talk to each other directly. Two browsers never chat with each other; both talk to the web server. Examples: the web, email, online banking, Facebook. Because one server cannot handle millions of users, big services use data centers with thousands of servers that look like one server from outside.

The problem with client-server: The server does all the work and pays for all the bandwidth. If a file of F bits must reach N clients, the server must upload N x F bits. When N grows, the server's upload link becomes the bottleneck. Servers and data centers are expensive to buy, cool and power. That is why companies spend huge sums on infrastructure and why a small server can crash when a news website suddenly gets millions of visitors after big news.

A worked number: Suppose a server must send a 100 MB update file to 1,000 clients. That is 100 x 8 = 800 Mbit per client, so 800,000 Mbit = 800 Gbit in total. With a 1 Gbps upload link, the server needs at least 800 seconds, more than 13 minutes, even if every client has a fast connection. Double the clients and the time doubles. In a P2P design, clients that already have parts of the file can upload them to others, so total upload capacity grows with the number of users. We will compute the exact P2P formula later in the course.

Peer-to-peer architecture: In P2P, there is little or no reliance on always-on servers. Peers, which are ordinary user machines, talk directly to each other. Each peer both requests and provides service. The big advantage is self-scalability: every new peer brings new demand but also new upload capacity. BitTorrent file sharing is the classic example. The downsides are management: peers come and go, have changing IP addresses, sit behind home routers, and are not all trustworthy. We will study P2P in detail in a later lesson; for now, know the trade-off.

Hybrids: Many real apps mix the two. Old Skype used servers to find users and then connected peers directly for calls. Many video call apps today try a direct peer-to-peer media path when possible and fall back to relay servers when home routers block it. Instant messaging often uses a server to know who is online, while the chat content may still go through servers. So in exams, if asked whether an app is client-server or P2P, it is fine to say hybrid and explain which part is which.

Processes, the real talkers: Strictly speaking, hosts do not talk; processes do. A process is a program that is running. Two processes on the same host talk using inter-process communication, which the Operating Systems course covers. Processes on different hosts talk by exchanging messages across the network. In each pair of communicating processes, the one that starts the conversation is called the client process, and the one that waits to be contacted is the server process. Even in P2P file sharing, during one transfer the downloading peer is the client and the uploading peer is the server.

Sockets, the door of the house: A process sends and receives messages through a software interface called a socket. Think of the process as a house and the socket as its door. To send a message, the process pushes it out of the door. On the other side, the transport layer infrastructure carries it to the door of the receiving process. The application developer controls everything inside the house, but has very little control on the outside: they can choose the transport protocol (TCP or UDP) and maybe a few parameters like buffer sizes. The socket is also called the API between the application and the network.

Addressing processes: To deliver a message to a process, you need two things: which host and which process on that host. The host is identified by its IP address, a 32-bit number in IPv4, like 172.217.194.100. The process is identified by a 16-bit port number. Popular server applications use well-known port numbers: HTTP uses 80, HTTPS uses 443, SMTP uses 25, DNS uses 53, SSH uses 22. So the full address of a web server process might be 172.217.194.100 port 443. Client processes usually get a random temporary port from the operating system, such as 51234, called an ephemeral port.

Port ranges in numbers: Port numbers go from 0 to 65,535 because 2^16 = 65,536. Ports 0 to 1023 are well-known ports, assigned by IANA to common services. Ports 1024 to 49151 are registered ports, used by specific applications, such as 3306 for MySQL. Ports 49152 to 65535 are dynamic or private ports, often used as ephemeral ports by clients. Exams like asking why a client does not need a well-known port: because nobody needs to find the client first; the client starts the conversation and tells the server where to reply.

What applications need from transport: Different apps need different things. Reliable data transfer: a file download or a bank payment cannot lose a single byte, while a voice call can live with a little loss. Throughput: a video stream may need at least 2 to 5 Mbps to look good, while email is elastic and uses whatever is available. Timing: a game or voice call needs low delay, maybe under 150 ms one way for comfortable conversation, while a file transfer does not care. Security: a payment app needs encryption and integrity. Thinking along these four dimensions helps choose the right transport.

TCP's services: TCP is connection-oriented: client and server exchange setup messages, a handshake, before data flows, creating a full-duplex connection. TCP provides reliable delivery: every byte arrives, in order, without duplicates. It also provides flow control so a fast sender does not overwhelm a slow receiver, and congestion control so senders slow down when the network is overloaded. TCP does not promise any timing, minimum throughput or, by itself, security.

UDP's services: UDP is lightweight and minimal. No connection setup, no reliability, no flow control, no congestion control. It just takes a message, adds port numbers and a checksum, and sends it. Packets may be lost or arrive out of order. Why would anyone use it? Because it is fast to start, has small headers, and lets the application decide how to handle loss. DNS queries, live voice, online games and the modern QUIC protocol run over UDP.

Security on top of TCP: Plain TCP sends bytes in clear text, so anyone on the path could read them. TLS (Transport Layer Security) is added on top of TCP, in the application layer, to provide encryption, data integrity and server authentication. When you see https and a lock in your browser, the HTTP messages are carried inside TLS over TCP. Apps use a TLS library, which offers its own socket-like interface. We look more at TLS in the security lesson.

Application-layer protocols: An application-layer protocol defines the types of messages (request, response), their syntax (fields and how they are separated), their semantics (meaning of each field), and the rules for when and how to send and respond. Some are open, defined in RFCs, such as HTTP and SMTP, so anyone can build compatible software. Others are proprietary, such as the protocols used inside many messaging apps. Do not mix the protocol up with the whole application: the web is an application; HTTP is just its protocol for moving pages.

Real life example 1, the Pathao app: When you book a ride, the Pathao app on your phone is a client. It sends requests with your pickup point to Pathao's servers, which are always-on and well-known. Drivers' apps are also clients that report their positions to the same servers. Riders and drivers never contact each other directly through the network for matching; the server matches them. That is client-server, using TCP with TLS because the data is personal and must arrive correctly.

Real life example 2, an online game: A PUBG or Free Fire match sends many tiny position updates per second. If one update is lost, the next one replaces it, so waiting for a retransmission would only add lag. That is why many fast games send such updates over UDP and handle loss in their own code, while login and in-game purchases use TCP and TLS. One app, two transports, chosen by need.

Common mistakes: Saying routers run applications. Saying P2P has no servers at all; many P2P systems use some servers for tracking or login. Mixing up the IP address (which host) and the port (which process). Thinking UDP is useless because it is unreliable; it is chosen on purpose. Thinking TCP guarantees speed or delay; it guarantees only correct, ordered delivery.

What exams ask: Compare client-server and P2P with examples, advantages and disadvantages. Define process, socket and port. Explain how a process is addressed. List the four service requirements of applications and match apps to them. Compare TCP and UDP services, and say which transport a given app uses and why. List well-known ports for HTTP, HTTPS, SMTP, DNS and SSH.

Recap: Network apps run only on end systems. They follow client-server, P2P, or a hybrid. Processes talk through sockets, addressed by IP address plus port number. Apps need some mix of reliability, throughput, timing and security. TCP gives reliable, ordered, connection-oriented delivery with flow and congestion control; UDP gives a bare, fast, connectionless service. TLS adds security on top of TCP. Next, we study the most famous application protocol of all: HTTP.
key_points: Network applications run only on end systems; routers never run app code.
Client-server: always-on server with a fixed address; P2P: peers both request and serve; many apps are hybrids.
Processes communicate through sockets, the door between application and transport.
A process is addressed by IP address plus 16-bit port number (HTTP 80, HTTPS 443, SMTP 25, DNS 53, SSH 22).
Ports 0-1023 are well-known, 1024-49151 registered, 49152-65535 dynamic (ephemeral).
Apps need some mix of reliability, throughput, timing and security.
TCP: connection-oriented, reliable, ordered, flow and congestion control; UDP: connectionless and minimal.
TLS runs on top of TCP to add encryption, integrity and authentication.
lessons.tip: Make a four-column table: app, needs reliability?, needs low delay?, TCP or UDP. Fill it with ten apps you use daily. Exams love 'which transport and why' questions, and this table trains the reasoning.

quiz.q: Which identifies the process on a host?
quiz.explain: The IP address picks the host; the port number picks the process.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of peer-to-peer architecture?
options: Self-scalability: new peers add upload capacity
Peers always have fixed IP addresses
quiz.explain: Every new peer brings demand but also capacity, so the system scales by itself.

quiz.q: Which service does TCP NOT guarantee?
quiz.explain: TCP gives reliable ordered delivery but no timing or throughput guarantee.

quiz.q: What is the well-known port of DNS?
quiz.explain: DNS uses port 53.

quiz.q: Why does a client usually not need a well-known port?
options: Ports are only for servers by law
The client starts the conversation and tells the server where to reply
quiz.explain: Nobody needs to find the client first; its ephemeral port travels in the request.

lessons.title: The Web and HTTP: Requests, Responses, Connections and Cookies
lessons.content:
Imagine you walk into a library in Dhaka and hand a slip to the librarian: 'Please give me book number 42 from shelf B.' The librarian goes, finds it, and hands it to you with a note: 'Here it is, returned by 15th.' You did not chat, you did not explain who you are; one slip in, one book out. Every time you open a web page, your browser does almost exactly this with a web server, using a protocol called HTTP, the HyperText Transfer Protocol.

What the web is made of: A web page is not one file. It is a base HTML file plus many referenced objects: images, style sheets (CSS), JavaScript files, fonts, videos. A news homepage can easily reference 50 to 100 objects. Each object is named by a URL, a Uniform Resource Locator. In the URL https://www.example.com/sports/cricket.html, the part https is the scheme, www.example.com is the host name, and /sports/cricket.html is the path name of the object on that host. The browser is the client, and the web server program, such as Apache or Nginx, is the server.

How it was before the web: Before 1990, the Internet already had email, file transfer (FTP) and remote login, but finding information meant knowing exactly which machine to connect to and which commands to type. Tim Berners-Lee at CERN combined three simple ideas: HTML for documents with links, URLs to name anything anywhere, and HTTP to fetch it. Because the browser handled everything, ordinary people could click links. The web turned the Internet from a tool for experts into a tool for everyone.

HTTP in one sentence: HTTP is a request-response protocol that runs on top of TCP, by default on server port 80, or port 443 when wrapped in TLS as HTTPS. The client opens a TCP connection to the server, sends a request message, the server sends back a response message containing the object, and that is one exchange. Because TCP is reliable, HTTP itself does not worry about lost packets; it simply trusts TCP to deliver the bytes in order.

HTTP is stateless: The server keeps no memory of past requests from a client. If you ask for the same image twice in a row, the server sends it twice; it does not think, 'I just gave you this.' This seems silly but is a deliberate design choice. Keeping state is complex: if the server or client crashes, the saved states may become inconsistent and need cleanup. A stateless server is simpler and can serve millions of clients. When an application does need memory, such as a shopping cart, it adds it on top, using cookies, as we will see.

The request message: An HTTP/1.1 request is plain ASCII text that people can read. Example:
GET /sports/cricket.html HTTP/1.1, then Host: www.example.com, then User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0, then Accept-Language: bn, en, then Connection: keep-alive, then an empty line. The first line is the request line: method, path, version. The next lines are header lines, each Name: value. The empty line marks the end of the headers. For GET there is usually no body; for POST the body follows, holding form data.

The methods: GET asks for an object; it is by far the most common. POST sends data to the server, such as a login form or a comment; the data travels in the body. HEAD is like GET but asks only for the headers, not the object, which is useful for checking whether something exists or has changed. PUT uploads or replaces an object at a given path. DELETE removes an object. Modern web APIs, called REST APIs, use GET to read, POST to create, PUT to update and DELETE to delete resources, so these methods are now as important for apps as for browsers. Note that GET can also carry small data in the URL itself, after a question mark, like /search?q=dhaka.

The response message: A response starts with a status line, then headers, an empty line, and the body. Example: HTTP/1.1 200 OK, then Date: ..., then Server: nginx, then Last-Modified: ..., then Content-Length: 6821, then Content-Type: text/html, then an empty line, then the 6,821 bytes of HTML. Content-Length tells the client exactly how many bytes the body has, so it knows where the object ends on the TCP byte stream. Content-Type tells the browser how to interpret the bytes: HTML, an image/jpeg, JSON and so on.

Status codes: The three-digit code tells the result. 1xx are informational. 2xx mean success: 200 OK. 3xx mean redirection: 301 Moved Permanently gives a new URL in the Location header, and the browser follows it automatically; 304 Not Modified is used by caches. 4xx mean the client made an error: 400 Bad Request means the server could not understand the message, 403 Forbidden means you are not allowed, 404 Not Found means no such object. 5xx mean the server failed: 500 Internal Server Error, 503 Service Unavailable, which you often see when a result website is overloaded on result day.

Non-persistent connections: In the earliest HTTP (version 1.0 by default), each object needed its own TCP connection. The client opens a connection, requests the base HTML, receives it, the connection closes; then for each of, say, 10 images, it opens a new connection, requests, receives, closes. Each new TCP connection costs a handshake. That is wasteful in time and in server resources, since every connection needs buffers and variables in the server's operating system.

RTT math for one object: Define RTT as the time for a small packet to go from client to server and back. With a non-persistent connection, fetching one object costs: one RTT to set up the TCP connection (the client sends SYN, the server replies, and the client's ACK can carry the request), one RTT for the request to reach the server and the first response bytes to come back, plus the file transmission time. So response time = 2 RTT + transmission time. Example: RTT = 50 ms, a 100 KB object over a 10 Mbps link takes 800,000 / 10,000,000 = 80 ms to transmit, so total = 100 + 80 = 180 ms.

Worked example for a whole page: A page has a base HTML file and 10 small images, transmission times negligible, RTT = 50 ms. Non-persistent, one at a time: each object costs 2 RTT, so 11 x 2 x 50 = 1,100 ms. Non-persistent with 5 parallel connections: the HTML costs 2 RTT, then the 10 images go in 2 rounds of 5, each round 2 RTT, total 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 RTT = 300 ms. Persistent connection with pipelining: 2 RTT for the HTML, then all 10 requests sent back to back, about 1 RTT for all of them, so 3 RTT = 150 ms. These numbers show why connection handling matters so much.

Persistent connections: HTTP/1.1 made persistent connections the default. The server leaves the TCP connection open after sending a response, and later requests and responses between the same client and server use the same connection. The server closes it after some idle time. This saves handshakes and lets TCP's congestion window grow, which we will understand later. Browsers usually open a few parallel persistent connections to each server to fetch objects faster.

Cookies, adding memory to a stateless protocol: A cookie system has four parts. First, a Set-Cookie header in the server's response, such as Set-Cookie: id=1678. Second, the browser stores the cookie in a file, linked to that site. Third, the browser sends a Cookie: id=1678 header in every later request to that site. Fourth, the server keeps a database entry keyed by 1678, holding your cart, login status or preferences. So the server can recognize you on every request without HTTP itself keeping any state.

What cookies are used for, and the worry: Cookies keep you logged in, remember your cart items, store language choice and help sites count visitors. But third-party cookies, set by advertising or tracking companies whose content is embedded in many sites, can follow you across websites and build a profile of your interests. That is why browsers now limit third-party cookies and why many sites show cookie consent banners. In exams, mention both the usefulness and the privacy concern.

Trying HTTP by hand: You can talk HTTP yourself. On a computer with telnet or netcat installed, connect to a site on port 80 that still allows plain HTTP, type GET / HTTP/1.1, then Host: and the site name, then press Enter twice. You will see a raw response with a status line and headers. Easier still, open your browser's developer tools (F12), go to the Network tab, reload any page and click a request: you will see the method, status code, request headers and response headers, exactly as described here.

Real life example 1, checking SSC results: On result day, thousands of students open the education board's result site at the same time. Your browser sends a POST with your roll and registration number. The server looks them up and replies 200 OK with an HTML page of grades. If the server is overloaded, you may see 503 or a timeout. If the URL changed and the old one redirects, the browser silently follows a 301 or 302. Every part of this lesson appears in those few seconds.

Real life example 2, staying logged in on Daraz: When you log in, the response includes Set-Cookie with a session ID. For the next weeks, every page request from your browser carries that cookie, so Daraz shows your name and cart without asking for the password again. If you clear browser cookies, you suddenly appear logged out, because the server no longer receives your session ID. Nothing changed on the server; only your browser forgot the cookie.

Common mistakes: Saying HTTP remembers clients; it is stateless, cookies are an add-on. Forgetting that HTTP needs TCP first, so the first object always pays an extra RTT. Mixing 301 (moved) with 304 (not modified). Thinking one page means one request. Writing the response time of a non-persistent object as 1 RTT. Confusing HTTP the protocol with HTML the document format.

What exams ask: Write a sample request and response and label each part. Explain the methods and common status codes. Compare persistent and non-persistent connections and compute the response time of a page for given RTT and object count, with and without parallel connections. Explain statelessness and how cookies work, with a diagram of the four components. Short note on URL structure.

Recap: A web page is a base HTML file plus many objects, each named by a URL. HTTP is a stateless request-response protocol over TCP, port 80 or 443 with TLS. Requests have a request line, headers and an optional body; responses have a status line, headers and the object. Non-persistent connections cost 2 RTT per object; persistent connections reuse one TCP connection. Cookies add state for logins and carts, with privacy trade-offs. Next we make the web faster with caching and look at HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and CDNs.
key_points: A web page is a base HTML file plus many objects, each named by a URL (scheme, host, path).
HTTP is a stateless request-response protocol over TCP, port 80, or 443 with TLS (HTTPS).
Requests: request line (method, path, version), headers, blank line, optional body.
Methods: GET, POST, HEAD, PUT, DELETE; REST APIs use them to read, create, update and delete.
Status codes: 2xx success (200), 3xx redirect (301, 304), 4xx client error (404), 5xx server error (500, 503).
Non-persistent HTTP costs 2 RTT plus transmission time per object.
HTTP/1.1 uses persistent connections by default, saving handshakes.
Cookies (Set-Cookie, browser file, Cookie header, server database) add state, but can enable tracking.
lessons.tip: Open the Network tab in your browser's developer tools (F12) and reload any site. Seeing real GET lines, status codes and Set-Cookie headers once makes this whole lesson stick.
lessons.task: A page has 1 HTML file and 8 images, RTT = 40 ms, transmission time negligible. Compute the load time with non-persistent serial connections, with 4 parallel non-persistent connections, and with one persistent pipelined connection.

quiz.q: What does status code 404 mean?
quiz.explain: 404 Not Found: the server has no object at that path.

quiz.q: Response time for one object with non-persistent HTTP is about:
quiz.explain: One RTT for TCP setup, one RTT for request and first response bytes, plus transmission.

quiz.q: How does a stateless HTTP server recognize a returning user?
options: Through a cookie ID sent in each request
quiz.explain: The browser sends the cookie the server set earlier, and the server looks it up.

quiz.q: Which method asks only for the headers of an object?
quiz.explain: HEAD returns the response headers without the body.

quiz.q: Which header tells the client how many bytes the body has?
quiz.explain: Content-Length gives the size of the body in bytes.

lessons.title: Web Caching and Modern HTTP: Proxies, Conditional GET, HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and CDNs
lessons.content:
Think of the corner grocery shop in your area. The shopkeeper does not run to the Karwan Bazar wholesale market every time someone asks for a packet of biscuits. He keeps popular items on his own shelf. Most customers get what they want instantly from the shelf, and only rare items need a trip to the wholesale market. The web does exactly the same trick, called caching, and together with newer versions of HTTP it is the reason pages load fast even though servers may be on the other side of the world.

What a web cache is: A web cache, also called a proxy server, is a network entity that answers HTTP requests on behalf of an origin server, the server where the object really lives. The cache has its own disk storage holding copies of recently requested objects. The browser is configured, or the network is set up, so that requests go to the cache first. The cache is both a server (to the browser) and a client (to the origin server). Caches are usually run by universities, companies and ISPs.

How a cache handles a request step by step: First, the browser opens a TCP connection to the cache and sends an HTTP request for an object. Second, the cache checks whether it has a copy. If yes, a cache hit, it returns the object to the browser at once. Third, if not, a cache miss, the cache opens a TCP connection to the origin server and requests the object. Fourth, the origin server sends the object to the cache. Fifth, the cache stores a copy and forwards the object to the browser on the existing connection. The next person asking for the same object gets a hit.

Why caching helps, the problem first: Imagine a university campus LAN of 1 Gbps connected to the Internet by a 15 Mbps access link. Students make 15 requests per second for objects of average size 1 Mbit, so the demand on the access link is 15 x 1 = 15 Mbps. Traffic intensity on the access link = 15 / 15 = 1.0. From lesson 2 you know what happens near 1: queuing delay explodes, in practice reaching minutes. Pages crawl. The campus has two options.

Option one, buy a fatter link: Upgrade the access link from 15 Mbps to 150 Mbps. Now intensity = 15 / 150 = 0.1, and the queuing delay on the access link becomes negligible. Total delay is roughly the Internet delay, say 2 seconds for objects coming from far away, plus milliseconds on the LAN. It works, but bandwidth to the Internet is expensive, especially international bandwidth, and the bill comes every month.

Option two, install a cache, worked: Install a cache on the campus LAN. Suppose the hit rate, the fraction of requests satisfied by the cache, is 0.4, which is typical. Now only 60% of requests go out: 0.6 x 15 = 9 Mbps on the 15 Mbps link, so intensity = 0.6. Queuing delay at 0.6 is small, say tens of milliseconds. Average delay = 0.4 x (LAN delay, about 0.01 s) + 0.6 x (Internet delay, about 2 s plus a little) which is about 0.004 + 1.2 = 1.2 seconds. That is even better than the expensive upgrade, and the cache costs much less. This worked example appears in many exams.

The freshness problem: A cache can hand you an old copy. If a news site updates its headline image, the cache might still serve yesterday's version. HTTP solves this with two tools. First, servers send headers such as Cache-Control: max-age=3600, meaning the object may be reused for one hour without asking. Second, after that, the cache can check with the origin server cheaply using a conditional GET.

Conditional GET: When the cache first fetches an object, the response contains Last-Modified: (some date). Later the cache sends a normal GET with an extra header: If-Modified-Since: (that same date). If the object has not changed, the server replies HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified with an empty body. The cache then serves its copy. If it has changed, the server replies 200 OK with the new object. A 304 response is tiny, so even when the cache must check, it saves sending the full object. Modern servers also use ETag, a version tag, with the If-None-Match header for the same purpose.

What a cache keeps and what it throws away: A cache's disk is limited, so it cannot keep everything forever. When it is full and a new object arrives, it must evict something. A common policy is LRU, least recently used: throw out the object nobody has asked for in the longest time. Popular objects keep getting requested and stay; one-off objects fade away. Caches also refuse to store some responses: personal pages marked Cache-Control: private or no-store, such as your bank statement, must never be served to another user. Getting this wrong would leak one person's data to another, so servers mark private content carefully.

Cache hierarchies: Caches can be stacked. Your browser cache sits on your device, a proxy may sit in your university or office, a bigger cache may sit at the ISP, and CDN servers sit closer to the origin. A miss at one level goes up to the next level instead of straight to the origin. Each level that hits saves traffic on all the links above it, just like a neighbourhood shop that gets stock from a local distributor instead of from the factory.

Browser caches: Your own browser also keeps a cache on your device. That is why the second visit to a site is faster: logos, fonts and scripts are already stored. The same freshness rules apply. When you press a hard refresh, the browser ignores its cache and asks the server again. Clearing browsing data deletes this cache, which is why sites feel slower right after clearing it.

HTTP/1.1 and head-of-line blocking: With HTTP/1.1, objects on one TCP connection are sent in order, first come first served. Suppose a page has one big video clip first and then several small images. The images must wait behind the video, even if they are tiny. This is called head-of-line (HOL) blocking. Browsers worked around it by opening several parallel TCP connections per server, usually up to about six, but that wastes resources and is unfair to other users, since each connection competes for bandwidth separately.

HTTP/2, frames and streams: HTTP/2, standardized in 2015, keeps the same methods, status codes and headers, but changes how they travel. Messages are cut into small frames, and frames of different objects are interleaved on a single TCP connection. Each request-response pair is a stream with its own number. So in our example, the server sends a frame of the video, then a frame of image 1, then image 2, then more video. The small images finish quickly while the video continues. HTTP/2 also compresses headers, lets the client set priorities for streams, and allows server push, where the server sends objects it expects the client to need, though push turned out to be rarely useful and browsers have since dropped support for it.

HTTP/3 and QUIC: HTTP/2 still has a problem: if one TCP segment is lost, TCP holds back all later bytes until the lost one is recovered, so all streams stall, not just the one that lost data. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, a transport protocol built on top of UDP. QUIC provides reliability and congestion control per stream, so a loss in one stream does not block others. QUIC also includes encryption from TLS 1.3 and combines the connection setup and security handshake, so a new connection often starts sending data after just one RTT, and repeat connections can sometimes send data immediately. Big services like Google and many CDNs already support HTTP/3.

HTTPS in one paragraph: HTTPS is simply HTTP carried inside TLS. Before any HTTP message is sent, the client and server perform a TLS handshake: they agree on encryption algorithms, the server proves its identity with a certificate, and they create shared secret keys. Then all HTTP data is encrypted. Caches in the middle cannot read HTTPS traffic, which is good for privacy but means a campus proxy cannot cache it in the old way. That is one reason the industry moved to CDNs, which are trusted by the website itself.

Content distribution networks: A CDN is a company or system that places many servers in many locations and stores copies of a website's content on them. When you request an object, DNS or other tricks direct you to a nearby CDN server instead of the origin. Two strategies exist. Enter deep: put small server clusters inside many access ISPs, very close to users. Bring home: build fewer large clusters at key locations such as IXPs. Netflix, YouTube and many news sites use CDNs. We will see in the DNS and streaming lessons how a client is pointed to the right CDN server.

Real life example 1, Facebook in Bangladesh: When you scroll Facebook in Dhaka, many of the images and videos you see are not fetched from the USA. They come from cache servers placed inside or near Bangladeshi ISPs and sometimes reached over BDIX. That is why a popular viral video plays smoothly even on a modest connection: millions of people get it from a nearby copy, and the international links carry only the first copy. It is the campus cache example, done at national scale.

Real life example 2, a university proxy: Some Bangladeshi universities have historically run proxy servers for their labs. A whole class opening the same course website in a lab session makes the first request a miss and the next fifty hits. The lab's international bandwidth usage drops, and pages open faster. The trade-off is that HTTPS sites can no longer be cached by such a proxy without breaking encryption, so modern setups rely more on CDNs and browser caches.

Common mistakes: Thinking a cache always gives the latest version; freshness depends on max-age and conditional GET. Mixing 304 Not Modified with 301 Moved Permanently. Thinking HTTP/2 changes methods or status codes; it changes only how messages are framed and multiplexed. Saying HTTP/3 runs over TCP; it runs over QUIC, which runs over UDP. Forgetting that the hit rate applies to requests, so only the misses load the access link.

What exams ask: Explain how a proxy cache works with a diagram. Solve the campus problem: compute traffic intensity with and without a cache, and average delay for a given hit rate. Explain conditional GET with If-Modified-Since and 304. Explain HOL blocking and how HTTP/2 framing helps. Compare HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. Short notes on CDNs and the enter-deep versus bring-home strategies.

Recap: Caches keep copies close to users, cutting response time and expensive access traffic. With hit rate h, only (1 - h) of the traffic crosses the access link. Freshness is managed by Cache-Control and conditional GET, which returns 304 when nothing changed. HTTP/1.1 suffers HOL blocking; HTTP/2 multiplexes framed streams on one TCP connection; HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP to avoid transport-level blocking and speed up setup. CDNs bring content close to everyone. Next we leave the web and look at email.
key_points: A web cache (proxy) answers requests on behalf of the origin server and stores recent objects.
With hit rate h, only (1 - h) of requests use the access link, lowering traffic intensity and delay.
Worked: 15 Mbps demand on a 15 Mbps link (intensity 1) drops to 0.6 with a 0.4 hit rate.
Conditional GET uses If-Modified-Since; the server replies 304 Not Modified with no body if unchanged.
HTTP/1.1 suffers head-of-line blocking; browsers open several parallel connections as a workaround.
HTTP/2 splits messages into frames and interleaves streams on one TCP connection, with header compression.
HTTP/3 runs over QUIC on UDP, avoiding TCP-level blocking and combining transport and TLS handshakes.
CDNs place content copies near users, using enter-deep or bring-home strategies.
lessons.tip: For cache problems, always write three lines: demand in Mbps, traffic intensity before the cache, and intensity after the cache as (1 - h) x demand / link rate. The rest is just averaging two delays.
lessons.task: Open your browser's developer tools, Network tab, and load a news site twice. On the second load, look for responses served 'from disk cache' or 'memory cache' and for 304 status codes, and count how many objects were not downloaded again.

quiz.q: A campus sends 20 Mbps of requests over a 25 Mbps link. With a cache hit rate of 0.5, what is the new traffic intensity?
quiz.explain: Only half goes out: 10 Mbps / 25 Mbps = 0.4.

quiz.q: What does a server send if the object has not changed since If-Modified-Since?
quiz.explain: 304 tells the cache its copy is still valid, with no body.

quiz.q: What is head-of-line blocking in HTTP/1.1?
options: The server refuses the first request
Small objects wait behind a large object on the same connection
quiz.explain: Objects are sent in order, so a big one delays the small ones behind it.

quiz.q: Which transport does HTTP/3 use?
quiz.explain: HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, which is built on UDP.

quiz.q: What does HTTP/2 change compared to HTTP/1.1?
options: It frames messages and multiplexes streams on one connection
quiz.explain: Methods and codes stay; framing, multiplexing and header compression are new.

lessons.title: Email: SMTP, Mail Servers, POP3, IMAP and MIME
lessons.content:
Think of how a letter travels through Bangladesh Post. You drop it in the post box near your house. Your local post office collects it and sends it to the post office in the receiver's area. There it waits in a pigeonhole or a P.O. box until your friend comes and picks it up, or a postman delivers it. Two important points: the letter waits at the receiver's post office even if your friend is not home, and different people handle the sending part and the picking-up part. Email works with almost exactly the same design.

What email is: Email is one of the oldest Internet applications, used since the early 1970s, and still essential for jobs, universities, banks and government services. It is asynchronous: the sender and the receiver do not need to be online at the same time. You can send an email at midnight, and your teacher reads it in the morning. Messages can contain text, attachments, images and links, and they can be sent to one person or to thousands.

The three main parts: The email system has user agents, mail servers and the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP). A user agent is the program you use to read, write, reply and forward mail: the Gmail app, Outlook, Thunderbird, or the webmail page in your browser. A mail server holds a mailbox for each user and a message queue for outgoing mail. SMTP is the protocol mail servers use to send messages to each other, and that user agents use to hand outgoing mail to their own server.

The journey of one email, step by step: Rahim in Dhaka sends an email to Karima, whose account is on a different mail provider. First, Rahim writes the message in his user agent and clicks send. Second, his user agent sends the message to Rahim's mail server, where it is placed in the outgoing queue. Third, Rahim's mail server, acting as an SMTP client, opens a TCP connection to Karima's mail server. Fourth, after an SMTP handshake, it sends the message. Fifth, Karima's mail server places the message in Karima's mailbox. Sixth, later, Karima opens her user agent, which fetches the message from her mail server. Notice the message does not go directly from Rahim's computer to Karima's.

Why servers in the middle: Why not send directly from Rahim's laptop to Karima's laptop? Because Karima's laptop may be switched off, offline, or sleeping. Mail servers are always on, so they can accept mail at any time and keep it until Karima reads it. Also, if Karima's server is temporarily down, Rahim's server keeps the message in its queue and retries, typically every 30 minutes or so, and gives up only after several days, sending Rahim a bounce message explaining the failure.

SMTP basics: SMTP is defined in RFC 5321 (the original was RFC 821 from 1982). It uses TCP on port 25 between mail servers. It is a push protocol: the sending side pushes the message to the receiving side. It is a direct transfer: the sending server talks straight to the receiving server, not through intermediate mail servers in normal cases. A historical limitation is that SMTP requires the message body to be 7-bit ASCII, so binary attachments must be encoded into ASCII before sending.

An SMTP conversation, worked: Lines starting with S are from the server, C from the client. S: 220 mail.example.com. C: HELO dhaka.example.org. S: 250 Hello dhaka.example.org. C: MAIL FROM: rahim at dhaka.example.org (written with angle brackets in real life). S: 250 OK. C: RCPT TO: karima at example.com. S: 250 OK. C: DATA. S: 354 Enter mail, end with a line containing only a dot. C: Do you like ilish? C: How about bhuna? C: a single dot on its own line. S: 250 Message accepted. C: QUIT. S: 221 closing connection. Each command gets a numeric reply code, much like HTTP status codes. Several messages can be sent over one TCP connection, so SMTP uses persistent connections.
