Reading SMTP reply codes: The first digit tells the story, just like HTTP. 2xx means success: 220 service ready, 250 action completed, 221 closing. 3xx means more input is needed: 354 asks the client to send the message text. 4xx means a temporary failure, such as 421 service not available or 450 mailbox busy; the sending server keeps the message in its queue and tries again later. 5xx means a permanent failure, such as 550 mailbox unavailable when the address does not exist; the sending server gives up at once and sends a bounce to the sender. So a typo in an email address usually produces a quick bounce with a 550 code, while a receiving server that is down produces delays and retries. Knowing this difference helps you understand those confusing delivery failure messages.

Comparing SMTP with HTTP: Both transfer files from one host to another, both use persistent TCP connections, and both use text commands and numeric codes. But HTTP is mainly a pull protocol: the client pulls objects from the server. SMTP is a push protocol: the sender pushes the mail. HTTP puts each object in its own response, while SMTP puts all parts of a message, text and attachments, into one message. And SMTP traditionally requires 7-bit ASCII, while HTTP has no such rule.

The message format: An email message, defined in RFC 5322, has header lines, a blank line, and the body. Typical headers are From:, To:, Subject:, Date:, Cc:. Do not confuse these headers with SMTP commands. MAIL FROM and RCPT TO are part of the SMTP envelope, used by servers to route the message, while From: and To: are inside the message and shown to the reader. They can differ, for example when you are in Bcc, and spammers abuse this difference to fake the From: line.

MIME, sending more than plain text: Plain RFC 5322 messages can only carry ASCII text. Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME) add headers like MIME-Version: 1.0, Content-Type: image/jpeg and Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64. Base64 turns every 3 bytes of binary data into 4 ASCII characters, so a 300 KB photo becomes about 400 KB of text, a 33% increase. A message with text and two attachments uses Content-Type: multipart/mixed, with a boundary string separating the parts. MIME also lets emails carry Bangla text using UTF-8, which is why you can write emails in Bangla today.

Mail access protocols: SMTP pushes mail to Karima's server, but Karima's user agent cannot use SMTP to pull mail out, because SMTP only pushes. So other protocols are used to retrieve mail. POP3 (Post Office Protocol version 3) is simple: the user agent connects to the server on port 110, authenticates with a user name and password, lists the messages, downloads them, and, in the common download-and-delete mode, deletes them from the server. IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol) on port 143 keeps all messages on the server, lets the user create folders on the server, move messages, search them and download only parts, such as headers. Secure versions run over TLS, on ports 995 for POP3 and 993 for IMAP.

POP3 versus IMAP in daily life: With POP3 download-and-delete, if you read mail on your office PC, the mail is no longer on the server and your phone will not see it. That was fine when people had one computer. Today you use a phone, a laptop and a lab computer, so you want the same mailbox everywhere, with the same folders and read status. IMAP keeps the state on the server, so every device shows the same view. That is why IMAP, or proprietary protocols with the same idea, won.

Webmail: Many people never use POP3 or IMAP directly. In Gmail on a browser, your user agent is a web page. Your browser talks HTTP (over TLS) to the Gmail servers to send and read mail. Between Gmail's servers and other providers' mail servers, SMTP is still used. So a webmail message from Gmail to a university address travels HTTPS from you to Gmail, SMTP from Gmail to the university server, and HTTPS or IMAP from the server to the reader.

Finding the receiver's mail server: How does Rahim's server know which machine handles mail for example.com? It asks DNS for the MX (mail exchanger) record of example.com, which names the mail server, then asks DNS for that server's IP address. We will see MX records in the DNS lesson. This is a nice example of one application, email, depending on another, DNS.

Spam and security: Original SMTP had no authentication: anyone could claim any From: address. Spam and phishing exploited this. Modern mail uses extra checks. SPF lets a domain publish, in DNS, which servers may send mail for it. DKIM lets the sending server add a digital signature to the message, which the receiver verifies using a public key in DNS. DMARC tells receivers what to do when these checks fail. Also, mail submission from user agents typically uses port 587 with authentication and TLS rather than port 25.

Real life example 1, a job application email: You send your CV as a PDF from your Gmail on your phone to an HR address at a Dhaka software company. The Gmail app uses HTTPS to Gmail's servers. Gmail's server looks up the company domain's MX record and connects with SMTP, usually protected with TLS. The PDF travels as base64 inside a MIME multipart message. The HR officer reads it in Outlook, which fetches it via IMAP or Exchange's own protocol. Every protocol in this lesson took part.

Real life example 2, the phishing message: A message says it comes from your bank and asks you to verify your account by clicking a link. The From: line shows the bank's name, but the message did not pass SPF or DKIM checks, so your mail provider marks it as suspicious or puts it in spam. Knowing that From: can be faked, and that the real sender is checked by SPF and DKIM, helps you avoid such traps.

Common mistakes: Saying SMTP is used to read mail; it is used to send and transfer, while POP3, IMAP or HTTP are used to read. Saying email goes directly from sender PC to receiver PC. Mixing the SMTP envelope with the message headers. Forgetting that SMTP originally needs 7-bit ASCII, which is why MIME and base64 exist. Saying IMAP deletes mail from the server by default; it keeps it.

What exams ask: Draw the email architecture with user agents, mail servers and protocols on each arrow. Write a sample SMTP dialogue. Compare SMTP and HTTP. Compare POP3 and IMAP. Explain MIME and base64 with a size example. Explain why mail servers are needed in the middle. Short notes on webmail, MX records, SPF and DKIM.

Recap: Email is asynchronous and built from user agents, mail servers and SMTP. SMTP pushes mail over TCP port 25 using commands such as HELO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, DATA and QUIT. Messages have headers and a body; MIME and base64 carry attachments and non-English text. POP3 and IMAP retrieve mail, with IMAP keeping everything on the server. Webmail uses HTTP for the user side. DNS MX records tell servers where to deliver mail. Next we study DNS itself, the Internet's phone book.
key_points: Email has three parts: user agents, mail servers (mailboxes and queues) and SMTP.
Mail goes sender agent -> sender's server -> receiver's server -> receiver's mailbox, never PC to PC.
SMTP uses TCP port 25, is a push protocol and uses commands HELO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, DATA, QUIT.
SMTP envelope addresses differ from the From: and To: headers inside the message.
MIME adds content types and base64 encoding so attachments and UTF-8 text can travel.
POP3 (port 110) usually downloads and deletes; IMAP (port 143) keeps mail and folders on the server.
Webmail uses HTTP(S) between browser and server, SMTP between servers.
MX records in DNS name a domain's mail server; SPF, DKIM and DMARC fight spoofing.
lessons.tip: Draw the Rahim-to-Karima email path with four boxes and label each arrow with its protocol: SMTP, SMTP, then POP3/IMAP/HTTP. That single picture answers most email exam questions.
lessons.task: In Gmail on a computer, open any received email, click the three dots and choose 'Show original'. Find the Received: lines, the SPF and DKIM results, and the Content-Type headers, and note which servers the message passed through.

quiz.q: Which protocol do mail servers use to transfer mail to each other?
quiz.explain: SMTP pushes mail from server to server over TCP port 25.

quiz.q: Why does email need base64 encoding for attachments?
quiz.explain: Binary data is turned into ASCII text; it actually grows by about 33%.

quiz.q: Which protocol keeps your folders and messages on the server for all devices?
quiz.explain: IMAP keeps mailbox state on the server, so every device sees the same view.

quiz.q: SMTP is described as a push protocol because:
options: The sending side pushes mail to the receiving side
quiz.explain: The sending server opens the connection and pushes the message.

quiz.q: Which DNS record tells a mail server where to deliver mail for a domain?
quiz.explain: The MX record names the domain's mail exchanger.

lessons.title: DNS: The Internet's Phone Book
lessons.content:
You do not remember your friends' phone numbers anymore. You tap their name in your contacts, and the phone finds the number. Computers on the Internet have the same problem in reverse. Routers only understand numeric IP addresses, like 142.250.193.100, but people want to type names like www.google.com or www.du.ac.bd. The Domain Name System, DNS, is the giant, worldwide contact list that turns names into addresses, billions of times every day, usually in a few milliseconds.

What DNS is: DNS is two things at once. First, it is a distributed database implemented in a hierarchy of many name servers around the world. Second, it is an application-layer protocol that lets hosts query that database. DNS runs over UDP on port 53 for normal queries, and can use TCP on port 53 for large responses and for copying data between servers. It is an application-layer protocol, but it is used by almost every other application, so it is often called core Internet infrastructure built at the edge.

Services DNS provides: The main service is hostname-to-IP-address translation. DNS also provides host aliasing: a complicated canonical name, such as relay1.west-coast.example.com, can have simpler alias names, such as www.example.com. It provides mail server aliasing: the MX record lets an email address like name at example.com work even though the mail server has a different name. And it provides load distribution: a busy site can have many IP addresses for one name, and DNS rotates the order of addresses in its replies, spreading clients across servers.

The problem with a central design: Why not have one big server with all names? Because it would be a single point of failure: if it crashed, the whole Internet would stop finding anything. It would have to carry an impossible traffic volume, since every host on Earth queries DNS. It would be far away from most users, adding delay. And keeping one huge database up to date for every new website would be a maintenance nightmare. In short, it would not scale. Before DNS, in the early ARPANET, all names were kept in one file, HOSTS.TXT, copied to every machine; that worked for a few hundred hosts, not for billions.

The hierarchy: DNS spreads the database over a tree. At the top are the root servers. Below them are top-level domain (TLD) servers, responsible for endings like .com, .org, .net, .edu and country codes such as .bd, .in, .uk. Below them are authoritative servers, run by organizations, holding the actual records for their own names. To find www.example.com, you could ask a root server for the .com servers, ask a .com server for example.com's authoritative servers, and finally ask the authoritative server for the IP of www.example.com.

Root servers: There are 13 named root server identities, a.root-servers.net through m.root-servers.net, run by 12 organizations. Each identity is actually many physical servers spread worldwide using a technique called anycast, so there are well over a thousand root server instances. Some instances are located in or near Bangladesh, which helps local resolution. Root servers do not know the IP of every website; they only know where the TLD servers are.

TLD and .bd: Each TLD is run by an organization, called a registry. Generic TLDs like .com are run by companies under contract. Country-code TLDs are run for each country; .bd is run in Bangladesh by BTCL, the Bangladesh Telecommunications Company. Under .bd there are second-level labels such as .com.bd, .edu.bd, .gov.bd, .ac.bd and .org.bd. So the university name du.ac.bd is read from right to left: bd, then ac, then du. Bangladesh also has the Bangla-script TLD .বাংলা, which shows that DNS can support names in other scripts through internationalized domain names.

Authoritative servers: Every organization with public hosts must provide authoritative records that map its names to addresses. A university can run its own authoritative DNS servers, or pay a hosting or DNS provider to do it. The authoritative server gives the final, official answer for names in its zone. Usually there are at least two of them, for reliability.

The local DNS server: Each ISP, university or company also runs a local DNS server, also called a default name server or resolver. It is not strictly part of the hierarchy, but it is central to how resolution works. When your phone connects to Wi-Fi, DHCP tells it the address of the local DNS server. Your phone sends every DNS query to this resolver, which does the hard work of talking to the hierarchy and caching the answers. Public resolvers such as Google's 8.8.8.8 or Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 can also be used.

Iterative resolution, worked: Your laptop wants the IP of www.du.ac.bd. Step 1: the laptop sends a query to the local DNS server. Step 2: the local server asks a root server. Step 3: the root replies with a referral: here are the .bd TLD servers. Step 4: the local server asks a .bd server. Step 5: the .bd server replies with a referral to the servers responsible for ac.bd or directly du.ac.bd, depending on how the zone is delegated. Step 6 and 7: the local server follows the referrals to the authoritative server for du.ac.bd. Step 8: the authoritative server replies with the A record. Step 9: the local server returns the answer to your laptop. In a simple three-level case this is 8 messages. The query from your laptop to the local server is recursive (please get me the final answer), while the queries from the local server to the hierarchy are iterative (tell me who to ask next).

Recursive resolution: In a fully recursive design, the local server asks the root, the root asks the TLD on its behalf, the TLD asks the authoritative server, and answers flow back down the chain. This puts heavy load on the root and TLD servers, so in practice the pattern is the one above: recursive from host to local resolver, iterative from the resolver onward. Exams often ask you to draw both and count messages.

Caching, the secret of speed: If every lookup went to the root, the root would melt. So every DNS server caches every answer it receives, for a time set by the record's TTL (time to live), for example 3600 seconds. If a hundred students in a hostel open the same news site within an hour, only the first lookup goes up the hierarchy; the rest are answered from the local server's cache in a millisecond. Local servers also cache the addresses of TLD servers, so in practice the root servers are rarely contacted. Your browser and operating system keep small DNS caches too.

The cost of caching: If a site changes its IP address, some resolvers may keep giving out the old address until the cached record's TTL expires. That is why administrators lower the TTL before moving a server to a new address. A short TTL gives fast updates but more queries; a long TTL gives fewer queries but slower changes.

Resource records: The DNS database stores resource records, each written as (Name, Value, Type, TTL). Type A: Name is a hostname, Value is its IPv4 address, for example (www.example.com, 93.184.215.14, A). Type AAAA: Value is an IPv6 address. Type NS: Name is a domain, Value is the hostname of an authoritative server for it, for example (example.com, ns1.example.com, NS). Type CNAME: Value is the canonical name for an alias, for example (www.example.com, web1.hosting.net, CNAME). Type MX: Value is the canonical name of a mail server for the domain. A TLD server holding an NS record for example.com usually also holds the A record of ns1.example.com, called a glue record, so the resolver can reach it.

The DNS message: Queries and replies share one format. A 12-byte header contains a 16-bit identification number, used to match replies to queries, and flags, such as query or reply, recursion desired, recursion available, and authoritative answer. Then come four sections: questions (the name and type asked), answers (records that answer it), authority (records of other authoritative servers) and additional (helpful extra records, such as the A record of an MX server).

Putting records into DNS: Suppose a startup in Dhaka registers bdbooks.com.bd. A registrar, a company accredited for that TLD, takes the request and fee. The startup gives the names and IPs of its primary and secondary authoritative servers. The registrar makes sure NS records and glue A records are entered into the TLD servers. The startup then adds its own A record for www.bdbooks.com.bd and an MX record for mail on its authoritative servers. From then on, anyone in the world can find the shop.

Try it yourself: On Windows, Mac or Linux, type nslookup www.du.ac.bd and see the address and which server answered. nslookup -type=mx gmail.com lists Gmail's mail servers. On Mac or Linux, dig www.google.com shows the full message with TTLs. Run the same query twice and notice that the second answer from your resolver may come faster and with a smaller TTL, because it was served from cache and the TTL is counting down.

DNS security issues: DNS was designed for a friendly world. Attackers can flood root or TLD servers with traffic (DDoS), though caching and anycast make this hard to succeed fully. Cache poisoning tries to trick a resolver into caching a fake answer that sends users to a fake bank site. DNSSEC adds digital signatures to DNS records so resolvers can verify that answers are genuine. Encrypted transports such as DNS over HTTPS hide queries from eavesdroppers on the local network.

Real life example 1, opening a site on a new phone: You buy a new phone, join home Wi-Fi and type prothomalo.com. DHCP has given you the router or ISP resolver as your DNS server. The resolver may already have the answer cached because your neighbours read the same news. If not, it consults the .com servers and the site's authoritative servers, which are often run by a CDN. The CDN's DNS may return the address of a cache server near your ISP, so the page loads from nearby. DNS here is not just a phone book but also a traffic director.

Real life example 2, when Facebook went missing: In October 2021, a configuration mistake withdrew the network routes to Facebook's own authoritative DNS servers. Resolvers worldwide could no longer find the IP addresses of facebook.com, and as cached records expired, Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp disappeared for hours. People in Bangladesh thought their internet was broken. The servers were still running; the phone book entries simply could not be reached. It is a powerful reminder of how central DNS is.

Common mistakes: Saying DNS runs over TCP only; normal queries use UDP port 53. Saying root servers know every IP. Confusing CNAME with A: a CNAME points a name to another name, an A record points a name to an IPv4 address. Forgetting the local DNS server. Calling the whole process recursive when the resolver-to-hierarchy steps are iterative. Forgetting that caching is what makes DNS fast.

What exams ask: Explain why DNS is distributed and hierarchical. Describe root, TLD, authoritative and local servers. Show iterative and recursive resolution with a diagram and count messages. Explain caching and TTL. Write sample A, NS, CNAME and MX records. Describe registering a new domain. Short note on DNS attacks.

Recap: DNS turns names into IP addresses using a distributed, hierarchical database of root, TLD and authoritative servers, with local resolvers doing the work for hosts. Host-to-resolver queries are recursive, resolver-to-hierarchy queries iterative, and caching with TTLs keeps it fast. Records A, AAAA, NS, CNAME and MX hold the data. DNS runs over UDP port 53 and supports aliasing, mail routing and load distribution. Next we see how P2P systems and video streaming share content at huge scale.
key_points: DNS is a distributed hierarchical database plus a protocol, mostly over UDP port 53.
Services: name-to-IP translation, host aliasing, mail server aliasing (MX) and load distribution.
Hierarchy: root servers, TLD servers (.com, .bd), and authoritative servers for each organization.
The local DNS server (resolver), learned via DHCP, does lookups for hosts and caches results.
Host-to-resolver queries are recursive; resolver-to-hierarchy queries are usually iterative.
Caching with TTL keeps DNS fast and takes load off root and TLD servers.
Records: A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), NS (name server), CNAME (alias), MX (mail server).
DNSSEC adds signatures against forged answers; DNS outages can make whole services vanish.
lessons.tip: Draw the iterative lookup for www.du.ac.bd as a star: your laptop and the local server in the middle, root, .bd and authoritative servers around it, and number every arrow. Counting arrows is a common exam mark.
lessons.task: Run 'nslookup www.du.ac.bd', 'nslookup -type=mx gmail.com' and 'nslookup -type=ns google.com' on any computer. Write down the IP addresses, mail servers and name servers you get, and which DNS server answered.

quiz.q: Which transport and port does a normal DNS query use?
quiz.explain: Ordinary DNS queries and replies use UDP on port 53.

quiz.q: What does an NS record hold?
options: The hostname of an authoritative name server for a domain
quiz.explain: NS points a domain to the name server that is authoritative for it.

quiz.q: What keeps root servers from being overloaded?
quiz.explain: Resolvers cache TLD server addresses and answers, so roots are rarely asked.

quiz.q: Which record maps an alias to a canonical hostname?
quiz.explain: CNAME maps an alias name to the canonical name.

quiz.q: In the usual pattern, how does the local DNS server query root and TLD servers?
quiz.explain: Root and TLD servers return referrals; the resolver asks the next server itself.

lessons.title: P2P File Sharing and Video Streaming: BitTorrent, DASH and CDNs
lessons.content:
Imagine the night before an exam, and one student in the hostel has the full set of photocopied notes. If everyone queues at his door, he spends the whole night handing out copies, and the last student gets them at dawn. Now imagine that every student who gets a few pages immediately lets others copy those pages too. Within an hour, the whole hostel has the notes. That simple idea, that receivers also become senders, is the heart of peer-to-peer distribution. The other half of this lesson is about the biggest traffic on the Internet today: video.

The distribution problem: A server must send a file of F bits to N peers. The server's upload rate is u_s, peer i's upload rate is u_i, and the slowest peer's download rate is d_min. Distribution time is the time until all N peers have the whole file. We will compare two designs: client-server, where only the server uploads, and P2P, where peers help each other.

Client-server distribution time: The server must upload N copies, N x F bits, so it needs at least N F / u_s seconds. Also, the slowest client cannot download faster than d_min, so it needs at least F / d_min seconds. Therefore D_cs is at least max(N F / u_s, F / d_min). The first term grows linearly with N. Double the users, double the time.

P2P distribution time: The server must upload at least one copy: F / u_s. The slowest peer must still download the whole file: F / d_min. And in total, N x F bits must be uploaded by someone, while the total upload capacity is u_s plus the sum of all u_i. So D_p2p is at least max(F / u_s, F / d_min, N F / (u_s + sum of u_i)). The key point: when N grows, the denominator grows too, because every new peer adds upload capacity.

Worked example: F = 100 Mbit, u_s = 10 Mbps, d_min = 20 Mbps, and each peer uploads at 1 Mbps. With N = 10: client-server = max(10 x 100 / 10, 100 / 20) = max(100, 5) = 100 s. P2P = max(100 / 10, 5, 1000 / (10 + 10)) = max(10, 5, 50) = 50 s. With N = 100: client-server = max(1000, 5) = 1000 s. P2P = max(10, 5, 10000 / (10 + 100)) = max(10, 5, about 91) = about 91 s. Going from 10 to 100 users, client-server time grew 10 times, but P2P time not even doubled. That is self-scalability in numbers.

BitTorrent, the classic P2P protocol: The set of peers sharing one file is called a torrent. The file is split into equal chunks, commonly 256 KB. A peer joining the torrent has no chunks at first; over time it collects them, and while downloading it also uploads the chunks it already has to others. Each torrent has a tracker, a server that keeps a list of participating peers, or the peers can find each other through a distributed hash table without a tracker. When a new peer, say Alice, joins, the tracker gives her a random subset of peers, maybe 50, and she opens TCP connections to some of them. Those connected peers are her neighbours.

Which chunk to ask for: rarest first. Alice periodically asks each neighbour for its list of chunks. She then requests the chunks that are rarest among her neighbours, the ones with the fewest copies. Why? If everyone grabbed the easiest chunks first, rare chunks might disappear when the few peers holding them leave. Rarest first spreads every chunk widely, so the torrent stays healthy even as peers come and go.

Whom to upload to: tit-for-tat. Alice cannot upload to everyone, so she gives priority to the neighbours who are currently sending her data at the highest rate. Every 10 seconds she measures this and picks the top four, called unchoked peers, to upload to. In addition, every 30 seconds she picks one extra neighbour at random and uploads to it, an optimistic unchoke. This lets newcomers with nothing to trade get started, and it lets Alice discover better partners. The result: peers that upload generously tend to get good download rates, and free riders are slowed down. It is like the hostel rule: share your pages and others will share theirs with you.

P2P problems: Peers leave suddenly, called churn. Many sit behind home NAT routers that block incoming connections. Some peers may be malicious and send fake chunks, so torrents carry a hash of each chunk to verify it. And P2P is often associated with copyright violations, although the technology itself is neutral: it is used legally for distributing Linux images, game updates and large scientific data sets.

Video, the elephant in the network: Streaming video is the largest share of Internet traffic. A video is a sequence of images, typically 24 to 60 per second, and each image is an array of pixels. Raw video would be enormous, so it is compressed by exploiting spatial redundancy (many neighbouring pixels in one image look the same) and temporal redundancy (consecutive images are very similar). Compressed bit rates vary widely: a few hundred kbps for low quality on a phone, a few Mbps for HD, and well over 10 Mbps for 4K. A bigger screen and higher quality mean a higher bit rate.

The streaming challenge: Throughput between server and client changes from second to second. If the video bit rate is higher than the available throughput, the playout buffer empties and the video freezes, the dreaded spinning circle. If it is much lower, the picture looks blurry for no reason. Also, users want playback to start quickly and want to skip forward. A good streaming system must adapt to the network.

HTTP streaming: The simplest method stores the video as an ordinary file on an HTTP server. The client sends a GET, receives bytes into a buffer, and once the buffer holds a few seconds of video, starts playing while the rest keeps arriving. The problem: every client gets the same encoding, regardless of whether it is on fiber in Gulshan or weak 4G on a bus in Gazipur.

DASH, adaptive streaming: Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP solves this. The video is encoded into several versions, each at a different bit rate, for example 300 kbps, 1 Mbps, 3 Mbps and 6 Mbps. Each version is cut into chunks of a few seconds. A manifest file lists the URL of every chunk of every version and its bit rate. The client first downloads the manifest, then requests chunks one by one with HTTP GET, each time choosing the version that fits its currently measured throughput and buffer level. If the bus enters a weak area, the next chunk is requested at 300 kbps; when the signal recovers, it moves back to 3 Mbps. The intelligence is entirely in the client.

A small DASH worked case: Throughput is measured at 2.5 Mbps and the versions are 1, 3 and 6 Mbps. A sensible client picks 1 Mbps, the highest rate below its throughput, so the buffer grows. After a few chunks the buffer is large and throughput rises to 4 Mbps, so it switches to 3 Mbps. If the buffer falls below a few seconds, it drops again. This is why the quality of a YouTube video sometimes visibly changes during playback.

CDNs for video: A single huge data center cannot stream to the whole world: it would be a single point of failure, the paths to faraway users would be long and congested, and the same popular video would cross the same long links millions of times. So video companies use content distribution networks, many server clusters spread geographically, as we saw with caching. With enter deep, small clusters are placed inside access ISPs, close to users, which gives the best delay and throughput but many sites to manage. With bring home, fewer large clusters are placed at key points, such as IXPs, which is easier to manage but a bit farther from users.

How a client is sent to the right CDN server: The common trick uses DNS. Suppose you click a video link whose host name is video.example.com. Your local DNS server asks example.com's authoritative server, which returns a CNAME pointing into the CDN's domain. Your resolver then asks the CDN's own DNS servers, which choose a nearby, lightly loaded cluster and return its IP address. Your client then streams the chunks from that cluster with DASH. The CDN may choose the cluster by geography, by measured delay to the resolver's network, or by load.

Real life example 1, Netflix and YouTube in Bangladesh: Large streaming companies place their own cache servers inside or near Bangladeshi ISPs. When a new popular drama or a cricket highlight is released, it is pushed to these caches during quiet hours. When you press play, DNS directs you to the cache in your ISP, DASH chooses chunks that suit your speed, and the international cables are barely touched. This is enter deep in action.

Real life example 2, sharing a Linux ISO in a university lab: The CSE department wants 60 lab PCs to download a 4 GB Linux image. If all download from one internal server with a 1 Gbps link, the server must upload 60 x 32 Gbit = 1,920 Gbit, about 32 minutes at best. If the PCs use BitTorrent among themselves, each PC also uploads chunks to others, the total upload capacity grows with the number of PCs, and the whole lab finishes much sooner. Many Linux distributions officially offer torrents for exactly this reason.

Common mistakes: Saying P2P needs no server at all; BitTorrent often uses a tracker. Forgetting the F / d_min term in distribution time. Thinking DASH means the server decides the quality; the client decides. Thinking a CDN is one big server; it is many clusters. Confusing rarest first (which chunk to request) with tit-for-tat (whom to upload to).

What exams ask: Derive and compare client-server and P2P distribution times, and solve a numeric example for two values of N. Explain BitTorrent: torrent, tracker, chunks, rarest first, tit-for-tat and optimistic unchoking. Explain DASH with the manifest file and rate adaptation. Compare enter-deep and bring-home CDN strategies. Show how DNS redirects a client to a CDN cluster.

Recap: In client-server distribution, time grows linearly with N; in P2P, peers add upload capacity, so the system scales by itself. BitTorrent splits files into chunks, requests rarest first and uploads tit-for-tat. Video is compressed and is the biggest traffic type; DASH lets the client pick the right bit rate chunk by chunk from a manifest. CDNs keep copies near users and use DNS to send each client to a good cluster. Next we write our own network programs using sockets.
key_points: Client-server distribution time is at least max(N F / u_s, F / d_min) and grows linearly with N.
P2P time is at least max(F / u_s, F / d_min, N F / (u_s + sum u_i)); peers add capacity.
BitTorrent: torrent, tracker, 256 KB chunks, neighbours, rarest first requesting.
Tit-for-tat: upload to the top 4 senders every 10 s, plus one optimistic unchoke every 30 s.
Video is compressed using spatial and temporal redundancy; bit rates range from hundreds of kbps to over 10 Mbps.
DASH encodes several bit rates in chunks; the client reads a manifest and picks each chunk's rate.
CDNs use enter-deep (inside access ISPs) or bring-home (few large clusters at IXPs) placement.
DNS with a CNAME into the CDN's domain sends each client to a nearby cluster.
lessons.tip: For distribution-time problems, always write the two or three terms separately, compute each, then take the max. Most lost marks come from forgetting one term, not from wrong arithmetic.
lessons.task: On YouTube, right-click a playing video and open 'Stats for nerds'. Watch the connection speed and the current resolution while you switch from Wi-Fi to mobile data or move to a weaker signal area, and note when the quality changes.

quiz.q: F = 100 Mbit, u_s = 10 Mbps, d_min = 20 Mbps, N = 10. What is the client-server distribution time?
Why does BitTorrent request the rarest chunks first?
options: To keep every chunk widely copied so it does not disappear
quiz.explain: Spreading rare chunks keeps the torrent complete as peers leave.

quiz.q: In DASH, who decides which bit rate to download for each chunk?
quiz.explain: The client measures throughput and buffer and chooses chunk by chunk.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of optimistic unchoking?
options: To give a random peer a chance and discover better partners
quiz.explain: It lets newcomers start and lets a peer find better trading partners.

quiz.q: Which CDN strategy places small clusters inside many access ISPs?
quiz.explain: Enter deep puts servers deep inside access networks, close to users.

lessons.title: Socket Programming: Writing Your Own UDP and TCP Client and Server
lessons.content:
So far we have studied applications that other people wrote: browsers, mail servers, DNS. Now it is your turn. Think of a socket like the counter window at a bank branch. The bank's internal work, vaults, ledgers and clerks, is hidden. You only see the window: you push a slip in, you get cash or a receipt out. A socket is that window between your program and the operating system's network machinery. Once you can open, use and close that window, you can build any network application, from a chat app to a small game server.

What a socket is: A socket is an endpoint for communication that the operating system creates for a process. Your program asks the OS for a socket, gives it addresses, and then sends and receives bytes through it. The OS kernel runs TCP, UDP and IP underneath. The interface we use, often called the Berkeley sockets API, came from BSD Unix in the early 1980s and is still used today in C, Python, Java, Go and almost every language, with nearly the same function names.

Two kinds of sockets: When creating a socket, you choose the transport. A UDP socket, created with type SOCK_DGRAM, sends independent datagrams with no connection; every message must carry the destination address. A TCP socket, created with type SOCK_STREAM, first sets up a connection and then gives you a reliable, ordered byte stream, like a pipe. The address family is usually AF_INET for IPv4 or AF_INET6 for IPv6. Choosing between them follows exactly the reasoning of lesson 4: does the app need reliability, or does it prefer speed and control?

Our example application: We will build the classic textbook application. The client reads a line of text from the keyboard, for example 'ami bhalo achi', and sends it to the server. The server converts it to uppercase and sends it back: 'AMI BHALO ACHI'. The client prints the reply. Simple, but it contains every important step: creating sockets, addressing, sending, receiving and closing. We will write it once with UDP and once with TCP, in Python 3, because Python's socket module mirrors the original API closely.

The UDP server: The server first imports the module with from socket import star (written as an asterisk). Then: serverPort = 12000. serverSocket = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_DGRAM). serverSocket.bind(('', serverPort)). This bind call attaches the socket to port 12000 on all of the machine's addresses, so that datagrams sent to that port are delivered to this socket. Then a loop: while True: message, clientAddress = serverSocket.recvfrom(2048); modified = message.decode().upper(); serverSocket.sendto(modified.encode(), clientAddress). recvfrom waits for a datagram of up to 2048 bytes and also returns the sender's address, an (IP, port) pair, which the server uses to reply.

The UDP client: serverName = '127.0.0.1' (or the server's IP or hostname). serverPort = 12000. clientSocket = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_DGRAM). message = input('Type a sentence: '). clientSocket.sendto(message.encode(), (serverName, serverPort)). reply, serverAddress = clientSocket.recvfrom(2048). print(reply.decode()). clientSocket.close(). Note that the client does not call bind; the operating system automatically assigns it an ephemeral port when it first sends. Also note encode and decode: sockets carry bytes, not text, so strings must be converted, using UTF-8 by default in Python, which also handles Bangla text.

What UDP does not do for you: In the UDP version, if the datagram is lost, the client waits forever in recvfrom. Real UDP clients set a timeout, for example clientSocket.settimeout(1.0), and retry or report an error when the timeout fires. If two datagrams are sent, they may arrive in the opposite order. Each sendto is one datagram, and each recvfrom returns exactly one datagram; message boundaries are preserved, unlike TCP. These are the trade-offs you accept for UDP's simplicity.

The TCP server: TCP needs a connection first, so the server has two kinds of sockets. serverSocket = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM). serverSocket.bind(('', 12000)). serverSocket.listen(1). This welcoming socket, sometimes called the listening socket, is like the front door where new customers knock. listen tells the OS to accept connection requests, with a small backlog queue. Then the loop: while True: connectionSocket, addr = serverSocket.accept(); sentence = connectionSocket.recv(1024).decode(); connectionSocket.send(sentence.upper().encode()); connectionSocket.close().

Welcome socket versus connection socket: When a client knocks, accept completes the TCP three-way handshake in the kernel and returns a brand new socket, the connection socket, dedicated to that one client. The welcoming socket remains open, waiting for the next client. Think of a restaurant: the host at the door (welcoming socket) greets each group, then a waiter (connection socket) is assigned to each table. With many clients, a real server handles each connection socket in a separate thread or process, or uses an event loop, so that one slow client does not block the others.

The TCP client: clientSocket = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM). clientSocket.connect((serverName, 12000)). sentence = input('Type a sentence: '). clientSocket.send(sentence.encode()). reply = clientSocket.recv(1024). print(reply.decode()). clientSocket.close(). connect starts the three-way handshake; when it returns, the connection is established. After that, the client does not mention the server address again with each send, because the connection already knows both ends. That is a big contrast with UDP's sendto.

A byte stream, not messages: A TCP socket is a stream. If the client calls send twice with 'hello' and 'world', the server's recv might return 'helloworld' in one call, or 'hel' then 'loworld'. TCP keeps the order and delivers all bytes, but it does not keep message boundaries. Real protocols therefore mark boundaries themselves: HTTP uses a blank line after headers and a Content-Length, SMTP ends data with a line containing only a dot, and many custom protocols put a length prefix before each message. Also, send may send only part of a large buffer; Python's sendall keeps sending until everything is gone.

Serving many clients at once: The simple TCP server above handles one client at a time. While it is busy with Karim, Rahima has to wait in the listen backlog. A common fix is a thread per connection. After accept returns, the server starts a new thread with the connection socket and goes straight back to accept. In Python: import threading, define a function handle(conn) that does the recv, send and close, and in the loop call threading.Thread(target=handle, args=(connectionSocket,)).start(). Now ten clients can be served at the same time. Very busy servers instead use an event loop, such as Python's asyncio, which watches many sockets and reacts to whichever one is ready, because thousands of threads would use too much memory.

Designing your own application protocol: Once the sockets work, you must decide what the bytes mean. Suppose you want a calculator server. You could agree that the client sends a line like ADD 5 7 ending with a newline, and the server replies with a line like OK 12, or ERR bad input. That is a tiny text protocol with a request format, a response format and an error rule, exactly the ingredients we listed for application-layer protocols. Text protocols are easy to debug, since you can read them, while binary protocols with fixed-size fields are more compact and faster to parse. Whatever you choose, write the rules down so that a friend could write a compatible client without reading your code.

The call sequence in one view: UDP server: socket, bind, then recvfrom and sendto in a loop. UDP client: socket, sendto, recvfrom, close. TCP server: socket, bind, listen, then accept in a loop, with recv and send on each connection socket, then close it. TCP client: socket, connect, send, recv, close. Drawing these four columns side by side is one of the most common exam questions on sockets.

Running it on one computer: Open two terminals. In the first, run python3 udp_server.py. In the second, run python3 udp_client.py and type a sentence. The client uses 127.0.0.1, the loopback address, which means this same machine; packets never leave the computer but still pass through the full UDP/IP code in the kernel. To try across two machines on the same Wi-Fi, replace 127.0.0.1 with the server laptop's IP, which you can find with ipconfig or ifconfig, and make sure the firewall allows port 12000.

Common errors you will see: Address already in use means another program, or your previous run, still holds that port; wait a little or choose another port, or set the SO_REUSEADDR option. Connection refused on a TCP client means nothing is listening on that IP and port, often because the server is not running or uses a different port. A client hanging forever in UDP usually means the datagram or reply was lost or blocked by a firewall. Permission denied when binding to ports below 1024 on Linux or Mac means those ports need administrator rights.

Where sockets sit in the stack: The socket API is the boundary between the application layer and the transport layer, the door from lesson 4. Everything above, such as the uppercase logic, is your application protocol. Everything below, such as TCP segments, retransmissions, IP routing and Wi-Fi frames, is handled by the operating system and the network. When you later use high-level libraries, like an HTTP client library in Python or the Dio package in Flutter, remember they are calling these same socket functions underneath.

Real life example 1, a campus chat server: A group of CSE students in Khulna write a small chat server for their lab. The server binds a TCP socket to port 5000 and accepts connections. Each student's client connects and sends lines of text; the server, using one thread per connection socket, forwards every line to all other connected clients. In about a hundred lines of Python they have a working chat room on the lab LAN. Add a length prefix to messages and a simple login, and it is a real application protocol of their own.

Real life example 2, a sensor sending readings: A student builds a flood-level sensor with a small board for a village near the Jamuna. Every 10 seconds it sends the water level, a few bytes, as a UDP datagram to a server. If one reading is lost, the next one comes soon, so UDP's lack of retransmission is fine, and the tiny overhead saves battery and mobile data. Choosing UDP here is a design decision, not a shortcut.

Common mistakes: Forgetting bind on the server, so clients cannot reach it. Calling recv on the TCP welcoming socket instead of the connection socket. Expecting TCP to preserve message boundaries. Forgetting encode and decode. Thinking the client needs a fixed port. Using sendto with a connected TCP socket or connect-less send with UDP without understanding the difference.

What exams ask: Write UDP and TCP client and server code for a simple task, such as uppercase conversion or adding two numbers. Draw the sequence of socket calls for UDP and TCP. Explain the difference between the welcoming socket and the connection socket. Explain why the UDP server needs the client's address for each reply while the TCP server does not. Compare the two in terms of reliability and message boundaries.

Recap: A socket is the program's door to the network. UDP sockets (SOCK_DGRAM) use sendto and recvfrom with explicit addresses and keep message boundaries but give no reliability. TCP sockets (SOCK_STREAM) use connect, listen and accept to set up a connection, then send and recv on a reliable byte stream; servers use a welcoming socket plus one connection socket per client. With these few calls you can build real applications. Next we look below the socket at what the transport layer really does: multiplexing and demultiplexing.
key_points: A socket is the interface between an application process and the transport layer, provided by the OS.
UDP sockets use SOCK_DGRAM; TCP sockets use SOCK_STREAM; AF_INET means IPv4.
UDP server: socket, bind, recvfrom, sendto; the client address comes with each datagram.
TCP server: socket, bind, listen, accept; accept returns a new connection socket per client.
TCP client: socket, connect (three-way handshake), send, recv, close.
TCP is a byte stream without message boundaries; UDP keeps each datagram separate.
Sockets carry bytes, so text must be encoded and decoded (UTF-8).
Clients usually get an ephemeral port automatically; servers bind to a known port.
lessons.tip: Type the four small programs yourself instead of copying them, then break them on purpose: stop the server, change a port, remove bind. Seeing each error message once teaches more than reading about it.
lessons.task: Write the UDP uppercase client and server in Python and run them on 127.0.0.1. Then change the server so it replies with the number of characters in the sentence instead, and test it with a Bangla sentence.

quiz.q: Which call returns a new socket dedicated to one TCP client?
quiz.explain: accept completes the handshake and returns a new connection socket.

quiz.q: Why does a UDP server need recvfrom rather than just recv?
options: To learn the client's address for the reply
quiz.explain: With no connection, each datagram's source address is needed to reply.

quiz.q: Which socket type is used for TCP?
quiz.explain: SOCK_STREAM gives a reliable byte stream, which is TCP.

quiz.q: A client sends 'hello' and then 'world' over TCP. What can the server's first recv return?
quiz.explain: TCP is a byte stream and does not preserve message boundaries.

quiz.q: What does 'Connection refused' on a TCP client usually mean?
options: No process is listening on that IP and port
The client did not call bind
quiz.explain: The server host answered that nothing accepts connections on that port.

lessons.title: Transport Layer Services: Process-to-Process Delivery, Multiplexing and Demultiplexing
lessons.content:
Imagine two big joint families, one in Rajshahi and one in Barishal, writing letters to each other. In each house there are twelve cousins. In Rajshahi, the eldest cousin, Anis, collects all the letters every week and gives them to the postman. In Barishal, the eldest cousin, Bithi, receives the bundle from the postman and hands each letter to the right cousin by reading the name on the envelope. The postal service moves letters house to house. Anis and Bithi move letters between the house and the right person. In networking, the postal service is the network layer, and Anis and Bithi are the transport layer.

What the transport layer does: The network layer, IP, provides logical communication between hosts: it delivers a datagram to a machine. The transport layer provides logical communication between processes running on different hosts: it delivers data to the right program on that machine. From an application's point of view, it is as if the two processes were directly connected, even though, in reality, there may be dozens of routers between them. Transport protocols run only in end systems. Routers in the middle look only at the network-layer header, not at the transport segment inside.

What the transport layer can and cannot fix: The services a transport protocol can offer are limited by the network layer below. If IP gives no delay guarantee, transport cannot promise a delay. But transport can add services that IP lacks. IP is a best-effort service: it does its best, but makes no promise that datagrams arrive, arrive in order, or arrive undamaged. TCP builds reliable delivery on top of this unreliable service, using sequence numbers, acknowledgements and retransmissions. It is like a courier that cannot make roads safer but can track every parcel and resend lost ones.

The two Internet transport protocols: UDP, the User Datagram Protocol, provides just two services: process-to-process delivery and error checking with a checksum. Nothing else. TCP, the Transmission Control Protocol, provides those two and adds reliable data transfer, connection management, flow control and congestion control. Both provide multiplexing and demultiplexing, which is the most basic job of any transport protocol and the topic of this lesson.

Segments: The transport layer on the sending side takes a message from an application, possibly breaks it into smaller chunks, adds a transport header to each chunk, and passes the result, a segment, to the network layer, which wraps it in a datagram. On the receiving side, the network layer extracts the segment and gives it to the transport layer, which processes it and delivers the data to the right process. The header carries, at minimum, two fields: the source port number and the destination port number.

Demultiplexing: A host may have many sockets open at once: a browser with several tabs, a WhatsApp connection, an email client, a music streaming app. When a segment arrives, the transport layer must decide which socket gets it. Delivering the data in a segment to the correct socket is called demultiplexing. It is Bithi in Barishal reading names on envelopes. The name on the envelope, in networking, is the port number together with addresses.

Multiplexing: On the sending side, many sockets produce data at the same time. Gathering data from different sockets, adding headers with the right port numbers, and passing the segments to the network layer is called multiplexing. It is Anis collecting letters from all the cousins and putting each in an envelope with the sender's name. Multiplexing and demultiplexing together let one network connection serve many applications at once.

Port numbers recap: A port number is a 16-bit number, 0 to 65535. Ports 0 to 1023 are well-known ports reserved for standard services: 80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS, 53 for DNS, 25 for SMTP, 22 for SSH. When you develop a new application, you must give the server a port number, usually above 1023. Clients usually get an ephemeral port chosen by the operating system. Each segment header contains a source port and a destination port, each 16 bits, at the start of the header.

Connectionless demultiplexing (UDP): A UDP socket is fully identified by a two-tuple: (destination IP address, destination port number). When a UDP segment arrives, the host looks only at the destination port, and the IP address already matched this host, and delivers the segment to the socket bound to that port. This has a surprising consequence: if two UDP segments come from different source IPs or different source ports but have the same destination IP and port, they go to the same socket. That is exactly what a DNS server wants: one socket on port 53 receives queries from the whole world.

What the source port is for in UDP: If the destination socket is chosen only by destination port, why carry a source port? Because it is the return address. When the server reads a datagram with recvfrom, it gets the client's IP and port, and it uses them as the destination of its reply. In our uppercase example, client A on port 51000 and client B on port 52000 both send to the server on port 12000. Both land in the same server socket, and the server replies to 51000 and 52000 respectively.

Connection-oriented demultiplexing (TCP): A TCP socket is identified by a four-tuple: (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port). When a TCP segment arrives, the host uses all four values to find the matching socket. So two segments with the same destination port but different source IPs or ports go to different sockets. This is how a web server on port 80 or 443 can talk to thousands of clients at once: each client connection has its own connection socket, distinguished by the client's IP and port.

Worked example: Host C runs a web server at IP 10.0.0.5, port 80. Host A, IP 10.0.0.1, opens two browser connections, from ports 26145 and 7532. Host B, IP 10.0.0.2, opens one connection, coincidentally also from port 26145. The server now has three connection sockets: (10.0.0.1, 26145, 10.0.0.5, 80), (10.0.0.1, 7532, 10.0.0.5, 80) and (10.0.0.2, 26145, 10.0.0.5, 80). The first and third share a source port, but the source IPs differ, so the four-tuples differ. The first and second share the source IP, but the source ports differ. Every segment finds exactly one home.

The welcoming socket again: Remember from socket programming that the TCP server also has a welcoming socket on port 80. Connection-setup segments, the SYN segments, are delivered to the welcoming socket, which waits for any source. When a connection is established, the operating system creates a new socket with the full four-tuple. After that, data segments from that client go to the new socket, not the welcoming one. In a table form, you could imagine the OS keeping a lookup table: four-tuple to socket.

Demultiplexing as pseudo-code: You can picture the receiving host's transport code like this. on_segment(seg): if seg.protocol is UDP: sock = udp_table.lookup(seg.dst_ip, seg.dst_port). If seg.protocol is TCP: sock = tcp_table.lookup(seg.src_ip, seg.src_port, seg.dst_ip, seg.dst_port); if not found and the SYN flag is set, sock = listening_table.lookup(seg.dst_ip, seg.dst_port). If sock is still not found, reply with an error: for TCP a reset segment, for UDP an ICMP port unreachable message. Otherwise append seg.data to sock's receive buffer and wake up the process waiting in recv. That last error case is what makes a client report 'connection refused', the error you met in the socket lesson.

Web servers, threads and processes: Some web servers create a new process for each connection, each with its own connection socket. Many modern servers instead use one process with many threads, or an event loop, and the many connection sockets all belong to that same process. Either way, demultiplexing works on sockets, not processes, so the four-tuple rule holds. Also note that with non-persistent HTTP, every object creates and closes a new socket, which adds load on busy servers, another reason persistent connections are preferred.

Port scanning: Because a server waiting on a port answers connection requests, anyone can try ports one by one to find which services a host runs. Tools like nmap do this. Administrators use it to check their own machines, and attackers use it to find weak services, such as an old database server exposed on the Internet. Knowing which ports are open is the first step to securing a server. That is why firewalls block all ports except those that are really needed.

Multiplexing at different layers: The idea of sharing appears everywhere. The link layer multiplexes different network protocols onto one link using a type field (for example, IPv4 versus IPv6 versus ARP in Ethernet). The network layer multiplexes TCP, UDP and ICMP into datagrams using the protocol field of the IP header (6 for TCP, 17 for UDP, 1 for ICMP). The transport layer multiplexes processes using port numbers. At each layer, a field in the header tells the receiver which upper module should get the payload.

Real life example 1, one phone, many apps: You are on a Grameenphone 4G connection with one IP address. Facebook Messenger, YouTube, Gmail and a bKash payment are all active. Each has one or more TCP or UDP sockets with different local ports, say 40001, 40002, 40003 and 40004. Segments arriving at your phone all carry your IP as destination; the transport layer looks at the ports (and for TCP, the full four-tuple) and hands each to the right app. Your video never shows up in your email.

Real life example 2, the BUET result server: On admission result day, a university web server on port 443 might handle thousands of simultaneous TCP connections. All of them have the same destination IP and port. The server tells them apart only because each client's IP and ephemeral port differ. Even students behind the same home router, sharing one public IP thanks to NAT, have different source ports, so their four-tuples still differ. We will see in the NAT lesson how the router makes sure of that.

Common mistakes: Saying routers do demultiplexing by port; only end hosts do. Saying a UDP socket is identified by four values; it needs only destination IP and port. Saying a TCP server needs a different port for each client; all use port 443, and the four-tuple separates them. Confusing multiplexing (sending side, gathering) with demultiplexing (receiving side, distributing). Forgetting that the source port is the return address.

What exams ask: Explain the difference between network-layer and transport-layer communication with the household analogy. Define multiplexing and demultiplexing. Compare connectionless and connection-oriented demultiplexing. Given several hosts with IPs and ports, list the sockets on a server and decide which socket each segment goes to. Explain why a web server can use one port for many clients.

Recap: The transport layer gives logical communication between processes, running only in end systems, on top of IP's best-effort host-to-host delivery. UDP adds only process delivery and a checksum; TCP adds reliability, connections, flow control and congestion control. Multiplexing gathers data from sockets into segments with port numbers; demultiplexing hands each arriving segment to the right socket. UDP sockets are found by destination IP and port; TCP sockets by the full four-tuple. Next we look closely at UDP itself.
key_points: Network layer: logical communication between hosts; transport layer: between processes.
Transport protocols run only in end systems; routers do not inspect segments for forwarding.
IP is best effort; TCP adds reliability on top, UDP adds only delivery to processes and a checksum.
Multiplexing gathers data from many sockets; demultiplexing delivers each segment to the right socket.
Every segment header has 16-bit source and destination port numbers.
A UDP socket is identified by (destination IP, destination port); the source port is the return address.
A TCP socket is identified by the four-tuple (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port).
One server port such as 443 can serve thousands of clients because their four-tuples differ.
lessons.tip: When a question gives several hosts and ports, draw the server as a box with one small box per socket and write each socket's tuple inside. Then route every segment by matching tuples; it turns a wordy question into a simple lookup.
lessons.task: With a browser open to two different sites, run 'netstat -an' and pick out the TCP lines in ESTABLISHED state. Write the four-tuple for three of them and check that no two four-tuples are identical even when the remote port is the same.

quiz.q: Which values identify a TCP connection socket?
options: Source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port
quiz.explain: TCP uses the full four-tuple to find the socket.

quiz.q: Two UDP segments from different clients have the same destination IP and port. Where do they go?
quiz.explain: UDP demultiplexes only by destination IP and port.

quiz.q: What is delivering segment data to the correct socket called?
quiz.explain: Demultiplexing happens on the receiving side.

quiz.q: What does the IP header's protocol field value 17 indicate?
quiz.explain: 17 means the payload is a UDP segment; TCP is 6, ICMP is 1.

quiz.q: Why does a UDP segment carry a source port?
options: It is used as the return address for replies
quiz.explain: The receiver replies to the sender's IP and source port.

lessons.title: UDP: The Simple, Fast, No-Promises Transport
lessons.content:
Think of shouting a quick message across a busy bazar to a friend: 'Ei, cha khabi?' You do not first ask whether he is listening, you do not wait for him to say 'got it', and if he did not hear, you just shout again. It is fast and has almost no overhead, but there is no guarantee. Compare that with sending a registered letter, where every step is recorded and you get a receipt. UDP is the shout across the bazar. TCP is the registered letter. In this lesson we study the shout, and why so many important applications choose it.

What UDP is: The User Datagram Protocol, defined in RFC 768 in 1980, is about as minimal as a transport protocol can be. It takes a message from the application, attaches source and destination port numbers and two small fields, and passes the segment to IP. IP tries to deliver it to the destination host, where UDP uses the destination port to hand the data to the right socket. That is the whole protocol: multiplexing, demultiplexing and a little error checking. No handshake, no acknowledgements, no retransmissions, no ordering, no flow control, no congestion control.

Connectionless: With UDP there is no handshaking between sender and receiver before sending. Each UDP segment is handled independently of the others. The first message the client sends can already contain real data. Compare TCP, where one full RTT is spent on the three-way handshake before any application data can go. DNS is the classic example: a DNS query is one UDP segment, the answer is one UDP segment, done. Doing a TCP handshake for every DNS lookup would at least double the time of every name resolution.

Why anyone chooses UDP, reason 1, control over timing: TCP's congestion control slows the sender down when the network is busy, and TCP keeps retransmitting a lost segment until it arrives, however long that takes. For a live voice call, a sound sample that arrives 2 seconds late is useless. Real-time applications prefer to send at a steady rate and accept a little loss. With UDP, the moment the application hands over data, UDP packages it and passes it to IP immediately.

Reason 2, no connection setup: As with DNS, no handshake means no setup delay. This is a major reason why QUIC, which powers HTTP/3, is built on UDP: it can design its own faster combined handshake instead of waiting for TCP's handshake and then TLS's.

Reason 3, no connection state: TCP keeps a lot of state per connection in the end systems: send and receive buffers, sequence numbers, congestion window, timers. UDP keeps none of that. A server using UDP can therefore support many more active clients with the same memory. That is why DNS servers, which answer huge numbers of short queries, and some game servers prefer UDP.

Reason 4, small header overhead: A TCP header is at least 20 bytes. A UDP header is only 8 bytes. For tiny messages, like a sensor reading of 10 bytes or a voice packet of 20 to 160 bytes, this difference matters. With a 20-byte voice payload, UDP plus IPv4 headers add 28 bytes, while TCP plus IPv4 would add at least 40.

The UDP segment structure: The header has four fields, each 16 bits, so 8 bytes in total. Source port number. Destination port number. Length: the number of bytes in the whole UDP segment, header plus data. Checksum: used by the receiver to check for errors. After the header comes the application data, for example a DNS query or a voice sample. Since Length is a 16-bit count of the whole segment, the minimum value is 8 (an empty message). In practice, with IPv4's 20-byte header and its own 65,535-byte maximum, the largest UDP payload is 65,535 - 20 - 8 = 65,507 bytes.

A worked header example: A client on port 51000 sends a 40-byte DNS query to port 53. The UDP header is: source port 51000, destination port 53, length 8 + 40 = 48, and a checksum. In hexadecimal, 51000 is C738 and 53 is 0035, so the first four bytes of the segment are C7 38 00 35, followed by 00 30 for the length 48. When the reply comes back, the ports are simply swapped: source 53, destination 51000.

Why a checksum: Bits can be flipped by noise on a link, or while sitting in a router's memory. Many link layers detect errors with CRC, but not every link on every path is guaranteed to do so, and errors can happen inside routers, where no link-layer check covers them. So the transport layer adds its own end-to-end check. This is the end-to-end principle: if a function must be guaranteed between end systems, it must be implemented at the ends, even if lower layers sometimes do it too.

Computing the Internet checksum, worked: You met the one's complement checksum in Data Communication; here it is in UDP's setting. The sender treats the segment as a sequence of 16-bit words, adds them with one's complement addition, meaning any carry out of the top bit is wrapped around and added to the bottom, and finally takes the one's complement (flips all bits). Example with three words: 0110011001100000 plus 0101010101010101 gives 1011101110110101. Add 1000111100001100: the sum is 1 0100101011000001, a 17-bit result. Wrap the carry around: 0100101011000001 + 1 = 0100101011000010. Flip every bit: checksum = 1011010100111101.

Checking at the receiver: The receiver adds all the 16-bit words, including the checksum. If no errors occurred, the result is all ones, 1111111111111111. If any bit is 0, an error has been detected. In our example, 0100101011000010 + 1011010100111101 = 1111111111111111. Correct. If one bit of the data had flipped, the sum would no longer be all ones, and the receiver would discard the segment or pass it up with a warning.

The pseudo-header: The UDP checksum is computed not only over the UDP header and data, but also over a pseudo-header taken from the IP layer: source IP address, destination IP address, the protocol number (17 for UDP) and the UDP length. The pseudo-header is not sent as part of the segment; both sides build it from the IP header for the calculation. It protects against a segment being delivered to the wrong host because of a corrupted IP address. In IPv4 the UDP checksum is optional (zero means not computed), but in IPv6 it is mandatory, since IPv6 itself has no header checksum.

What the checksum cannot do: The checksum detects many errors but not all. For example, if two 16-bit words are swapped, the sum is the same, so the error is invisible. If one bit flips from 0 to 1 in one word and the same bit position flips from 1 to 0 in another, the errors cancel out. And UDP does nothing to recover: it simply drops or flags the damaged segment. Recovery, if needed, is the application's job.

Reliability in the application: An application can use UDP and still be reliable, by adding acknowledgements and retransmissions in its own code. This gives full control: for example, a game can retransmit important events like 'player picked up the item' but not unimportant ones like an old position. QUIC is the big modern example: it adds reliability, ordering per stream, congestion control and encryption on top of UDP, all in user-space code that can be updated without changing the operating system.

The danger of UDP: Because UDP has no congestion control, a sender can blast traffic as fast as it wants. If many UDP video streams did this on a crowded link, routers would overflow, losses would soar, and TCP flows, which politely slow down, would be squeezed out. This is a real concern, so well-behaved UDP applications, such as video conferencing tools and QUIC, implement their own congestion control. UDP is also used in DDoS reflection attacks, where an attacker sends small queries with a faked source IP to servers that send much larger replies to the victim.

Applications and their transports: Email (SMTP), remote login (SSH), the web (HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2) and file transfer use TCP, because they need reliability. DNS uses UDP, mostly. Network management (SNMP) uses UDP because it must work even when the network is in trouble. Internet telephony and video conferencing typically use UDP, often with RTP on top. Streaming services like YouTube and Netflix usually run over TCP with DASH, while HTTP/3 and QUIC put more and more web and video traffic onto UDP. Online games use UDP for fast state updates.

Real life example 1, a WhatsApp voice call from Chattogram to Dubai: Many Bangladeshi families talk to relatives working in the Gulf every day. During the call, voice is cut into small packets every few tens of milliseconds and sent typically over UDP. If a packet is lost, the app may stretch the neighbouring sound slightly or play a moment of silence. Nobody wants the call to pause while a lost packet is retransmitted from Dubai. The call quality is a little imperfect but always live.

Real life example 2, DNS lookups on a slow connection: On a weak mobile connection in a village, each new site needs a DNS lookup first. With UDP, it is a single round trip to the resolver. If the reply does not come within a timeout, the phone simply asks again, maybe a different resolver. Using TCP would add a handshake round trip to every lookup, making browsing noticeably slower. Here simplicity directly saves time.

Common mistakes: Saying UDP has no error checking; it has a checksum, it just does not recover. Saying UDP guarantees order. Forgetting that the UDP length field includes the 8-byte header. Forgetting the wrap-around carry in checksum addition, or forgetting the final bit flip. Saying the checksum detects all errors. Saying video streaming always uses UDP; many streaming services use TCP with DASH.

What exams ask: List UDP's services and the reasons to prefer UDP over TCP. Draw the UDP header with field sizes. Compute the length field for a given payload. Compute a checksum for three 16-bit words and verify it at the receiver. Explain why UDP has a checksum when links already have CRC. Name applications that use UDP and explain why.

Recap: UDP is connectionless and minimal: ports for multiplexing, a length field and a checksum, in an 8-byte header. It offers no reliability, ordering, flow control or congestion control. Applications choose it for timing control, no setup delay, no connection state and low overhead, and some add reliability themselves, like QUIC. The checksum uses one's complement addition with wrap-around, then flips the bits; the receiver checks for all ones. Next we ask the big question: how can we build reliable delivery over an unreliable channel?
key_points: UDP (RFC 768) adds only port-based multiplexing and a checksum on top of IP.
UDP is connectionless: no handshake, no ACKs, no retransmission, no ordering, no flow or congestion control.
Reasons to use UDP: timing control, no setup delay, no connection state, small 8-byte header.
UDP header: source port, destination port, length (header + data), checksum, each 16 bits.
Checksum: one's complement sum of 16-bit words with wrap-around carry, then flip all bits.
The receiver adds everything including the checksum and expects all ones.
The checksum also covers a pseudo-header of IP addresses, protocol and length; mandatory in IPv6.
DNS, VoIP, games, SNMP and QUIC use UDP; apps can add their own reliability.
lessons.tip: Practise the checksum with only 4-bit words first, for example 0110 + 1011 + 0101, so the wrap-around and bit flip become automatic. Then 16-bit exam questions are just longer, not harder.
lessons.task: Compute the one's complement checksum of the three 16-bit words 1100110011001100, 0101010101010101 and 0000111100001111 by hand. Then add the checksum to the sum and verify that you get all ones.

quiz.q: How many bytes is the UDP header?
quiz.explain: Four 16-bit fields: 4 x 2 = 8 bytes.

quiz.q: A UDP segment carries 100 bytes of data. What is the value of its Length field?
quiz.explain: Length counts header plus data: 8 + 100 = 108.

quiz.q: When the receiver adds all 16-bit words including the checksum and gets no error, the result is:
quiz.explain: With no detected error, the one's complement sum is 1111111111111111.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a reason to choose UDP?
options: No connection state on the server
quiz.explain: UDP gives no ordering guarantee; that is a TCP service.

quiz.q: Why does UDP include a checksum even though many links use CRC?
options: Not every link or router memory is protected, so an end-to-end check is needed
quiz.explain: The end-to-end principle: errors can occur where no link check covers them.

lessons.title: Principles of Reliable Data Transfer: From rdt1.0 to Pipelining
lessons.content:
Imagine dictating your exam roll number to a friend over a bad phone line during a storm in Sylhet. You say 'two seven', but the line crackles. Your friend says 'what?'. You repeat. Then you say 'four', and hear nothing back; did he hear it, or did his reply get lost? Should you repeat 'four'? If you repeat and he already wrote it down, he might write 'four four'. Building a reliable conversation over an unreliable line is surprisingly tricky. Computer networks face exactly this problem, and in this lesson we build the solution step by step, one problem at a time.

The goal: The application above wants a reliable channel: no bits corrupted, no data lost, everything delivered in the order sent. That is the service TCP provides. But the channel below, IP, is unreliable: it may flip bits, lose packets, and in general reorder them. Our job is to design a reliable data transfer protocol, rdt, sitting between them. We will consider only one direction of data, from sender to receiver, though control packets like acknowledgements flow back. We describe each version in words; textbooks draw them as finite state machines.

rdt1.0, a perfectly reliable channel: Suppose the channel never flips bits and never loses packets. Then the protocol is trivial. The sender takes data from above, makes a packet and sends it. The receiver takes the packet, extracts the data and delivers it up. No feedback is needed, since nothing can go wrong. This is our starting point, like talking face to face in a quiet room.

rdt2.0, a channel with bit errors: Now suppose bits can be flipped, but packets are never lost. How do people handle this on the phone? The listener says 'OK' when a message is understood and 'please repeat' when it is not. Protocols based on this are called ARQ, Automatic Repeat reQuest, protocols. They need three things. Error detection: a checksum so the receiver knows bits flipped. Receiver feedback: positive acknowledgements (ACK) and negative acknowledgements (NAK). Retransmission: the sender resends a packet that was received in error.

How rdt2.0 works: The sender sends a packet with a checksum and then waits. If an ACK comes back, it moves on to the next piece of data. If a NAK comes back, it resends the same packet and waits again. While waiting, it does not accept new data from above. Such a protocol is called stop-and-wait. The receiver checks the checksum: if fine, it delivers the data and sends ACK; if corrupted, it sends NAK.

The fatal flaw of rdt2.0: What if the ACK or NAK itself is corrupted? The sender cannot tell whether the receiver got the data right. If it simply resends, the receiver might receive a duplicate and deliver the same data twice, like your friend writing 'four four'. If it does not resend, data might be lost. We need a way for the receiver to recognise a duplicate.

rdt2.1, sequence numbers: The solution is to number each data packet. With stop-and-wait, a 1-bit sequence number is enough: packets alternate 0, 1, 0, 1. If the sender gets a garbled ACK/NAK, it simply resends the current packet. The receiver looks at the sequence number: if it is expecting packet 1 but receives packet 0 again, it knows this is a duplicate, discards the data, and sends an ACK so the sender can move on. Both sides now have two states each, waiting for 0 or for 1.

rdt2.2, NAK-free: We can remove NAKs entirely. Instead of sending a NAK, the receiver sends an ACK for the last correctly received packet, and the ACK carries the sequence number it acknowledges. If the sender is waiting for ACK 1 but receives ACK 0, a duplicate ACK, it knows packet 1 was not received correctly and resends it. A duplicate ACK means the same as a NAK. This is important because TCP works this way: it has no NAKs, only ACKs, and treats duplicate ACKs as a hint of trouble.

rdt3.0, a channel with errors and loss: Now packets themselves can disappear, data or ACKs. Two new questions: how to detect loss, and what to do. The answer is a countdown timer. The sender waits a reasonable amount of time for an ACK. If none arrives before the timer expires, it retransmits. The receiver does nothing new. If the packet was only delayed, not lost, the retransmission creates a duplicate, but sequence numbers already handle duplicates. The sender must start the timer each time it sends a packet, react to timeouts, and stop the timer when the correct ACK arrives.

How long to wait: The timer must be at least one round-trip time plus the processing time at the receiver, otherwise the sender retransmits needlessly. But if it is too long, recovery from real loss is slow. In practice, the sender picks a value judged likely to cover the RTT and accepts that sometimes it will retransmit unnecessarily.
