We will see how TCP estimates this value in the next lesson.

The four scenarios of rdt3.0: Scenario 1, no loss: pkt0, ack0, pkt1, ack1, smooth. Scenario 2, lost packet: pkt1 is lost; the timer expires; the sender resends pkt1; the receiver ACKs it. Scenario 3, lost ACK: pkt1 arrives, ack1 is lost; timeout; the sender resends pkt1; the receiver sees a duplicate 1, discards it, resends ack1. Scenario 4, premature timeout: ack1 is just slow; the sender times out and resends pkt1; then the original ack1 arrives and the sender sends pkt0; then a second ack1 arrives and is ignored. Because sequence numbers alternate between 0 and 1, rdt3.0 is also called the alternating-bit protocol. Drawing these four timelines is a classic exam question.

rdt3.0 works, but it is painfully slow: Consider two hosts, one on each side of a continent, RTT = 30 ms, link rate R = 1 Gbps, packets of L = 1,000 bytes = 8,000 bits. Transmission time L/R = 8,000 / 10^9 = 8 microseconds. With stop-and-wait, the sender sends one packet, which takes 0.008 ms, and then waits for the ACK, about 30 ms. Sender utilization, the fraction of time the sender is actually sending, is U = (L/R) / (RTT + L/R) = 0.008 / 30.008, about 0.00027. The effective throughput is 8,000 bits per 30.008 ms, about 267 kbps, on a 1 Gbps link! A protocol can ruin the best hardware.

Pipelining, the fix: Instead of sending one packet and waiting, let the sender send several packets without waiting for acknowledgements, filling the pipe. If the sender can send 3 packets per RTT, utilization triples: U = 3 x 0.008 / 30.008, about 0.0008. To fully use the 1 Gbps link, the sender would need about 30.008 / 0.008, roughly 3,750 packets in flight. Pipelining has consequences: sequence numbers must have a larger range, since many packets are in flight at once; the sender must buffer all sent but unacknowledged packets; and the receiver may need to buffer too. How lost and out-of-order packets are handled decides which pipelined protocol we use.

Go-Back-N, a recap: You studied Go-Back-N in Data Communication, so here we keep it short. The sender may have up to N unacknowledged packets, a window of size N sliding over the sequence numbers. ACKs are cumulative: ACK n means all packets up to and including n arrived correctly. There is one timer, for the oldest unacknowledged packet. On timeout, the sender resends all packets in the window that have not been acknowledged, which is why it is called go back N. The receiver keeps no buffer for out-of-order packets: it discards them and re-ACKs the last in-order packet. Simple receiver, but a single loss can cause many retransmissions.

GBN worked example: Window N = 4, packets 0 to 7. The sender sends 0, 1, 2, 3. Packet 2 is lost. The receiver gets 0 and 1 and ACKs them; then it gets 3, which is out of order, so it discards it and sends ACK 1 again. The sender, after ACKs 0 and 1, slides its window and sends 4 and 5; the receiver discards them too, sending ACK 1 each time. When the timer for packet 2 expires, the sender resends 2, 3, 4 and 5. Four packets were resent to repair one loss.

Selective Repeat, a recap: In Selective Repeat, the receiver individually acknowledges each correctly received packet, even if out of order, and buffers out-of-order packets until the missing ones arrive, then delivers them in order. The sender keeps a timer per packet and retransmits only those packets that are suspected lost. In the example above, only packet 2 would be resent. The cost is more buffering and per-packet timers. One rule to remember: with sequence numbers in a space of size k, the window size must be at most k/2 for Selective Repeat, otherwise the receiver cannot tell a new packet from a retransmission of an old one. For Go-Back-N the window must be at most k - 1.

Reordering in the real network: Our rdt3.0 assumed the channel does not reorder packets. In the Internet, packets can take different paths and arrive out of order, and an old copy of a packet with sequence number x could appear long after x has been reused. Real protocols handle this by making the sequence number space very large and assuming a maximum packet lifetime in the network. TCP's 32-bit byte-based sequence numbers and an assumed maximum segment lifetime of a couple of minutes serve exactly this purpose.

Real life example 1, bKash transaction confirmations: When you send money, your app sends a request and waits for a confirmation. If no confirmation arrives within a time limit, it does not simply send a second payment; it checks the transaction status or uses a transaction ID so a retry is recognised as a duplicate. That is rdt3.0's logic at the application level: timeouts to detect loss, and identifiers like sequence numbers to avoid doing the same thing twice.

Real life example 2, a shipment of exam scripts: A board office sends 20 boxes of answer scripts from Dhaka to Rangpur by truck, numbered 1 to 20. The Rangpur office signs and returns a receipt listing boxes received. If box 7 is missing, Go-Back-N thinking would resend boxes 7 to 20; Selective Repeat thinking would resend only box 7. Numbering the boxes is what makes any recovery possible.

Common mistakes: Forgetting that ACKs and NAKs can be corrupted too, which is the reason for sequence numbers. Thinking the timer handles corrupted packets; checksums handle corruption, timers handle loss. Computing utilization as L/R divided by RTT alone, forgetting to add L/R in the denominator. Mixing up GBN (cumulative ACK, single timer, resend all) with SR (individual ACKs, per-packet timers, resend one). Forgetting the window size limits.

What exams ask: Explain the evolution from rdt1.0 to rdt3.0, stating which problem each version solves and how. Draw rdt3.0 timelines for packet loss, ACK loss and premature timeout. Compute stop-and-wait utilization and throughput for given L, R and RTT, and the improvement with a window of N packets. Trace GBN and SR for a given loss pattern. State the window size constraints.

Recap: Reliable transfer over an unreliable channel needs checksums for errors, ACKs for feedback, sequence numbers to spot duplicates, and timers to detect loss. rdt2.2 shows that duplicate ACKs can replace NAKs; rdt3.0 is the alternating-bit protocol. Stop-and-wait wastes almost all the capacity of fast, long links, so real protocols pipeline using Go-Back-N or Selective Repeat ideas. Next we see how TCP combines these ideas into the protocol that carries most Internet traffic.
key_points: Reliable transfer needs error detection, receiver feedback (ACK), retransmission, sequence numbers and timers.
rdt2.0 adds ACK/NAK; rdt2.1 adds 1-bit sequence numbers to detect duplicates when ACKs are garbled.
rdt2.2 removes NAKs: a duplicate ACK for the previous packet acts as a NAK.
rdt3.0 adds a countdown timer to recover from loss; it is the alternating-bit protocol.
Stop-and-wait utilization U = (L/R) / (RTT + L/R); worked: 0.00027 on a 1 Gbps, 30 ms link.
Pipelining sends many packets before ACKs; N packets per RTT multiply utilization by N.
Go-Back-N: cumulative ACKs, one timer, resend the whole window; window at most k - 1.
Selective Repeat: individual ACKs, buffering, per-packet timers; window at most k/2.
lessons.tip: Draw every rdt and GBN/SR question as two vertical timelines with slanted arrows, and label each arrow pkt or ack with its number. Lost packets get an X in the middle. Timelines make the logic visible and earn easy marks.
lessons.task: Compute the stop-and-wait utilization and throughput for L = 1,500 bytes, R = 100 Mbps and RTT = 50 ms. Then find how many packets must be in flight to reach at least 90% utilization.

quiz.q: Which problem do sequence numbers solve in rdt2.1?
options: Recognising duplicate packets when ACK/NAK is corrupted
quiz.explain: If the sender resends after a garbled ACK, the receiver needs numbers to spot the duplicate.

quiz.q: What does rdt3.0 add to handle lost packets?
quiz.explain: A timeout tells the sender to resend if no ACK arrives in time.

quiz.q: L = 8,000 bits, R = 1 Gbps, RTT = 30 ms. Stop-and-wait utilization is about:
In Go-Back-N, what happens when the timer for the oldest packet expires?
options: All sent but unacknowledged packets are resent
quiz.explain: GBN goes back and resends every unacknowledged packet in the window.

quiz.q: With sequence numbers 0 to 7 (k = 8), what is the maximum Selective Repeat window?
quiz.explain: For SR the window must be at most k/2 = 4.

lessons.title: TCP Basics: Segments, Sequence Numbers, ACKs, Timeouts and Fast Retransmit
lessons.content:
Imagine you are copying a long Bangla novel for a friend, page by page, and posting the pages one envelope at a time. You number every character of the book, not just the pages, so if your friend says 'I have everything up to character 5,000', you know exactly where to continue, even if your envelopes were different sizes. If an envelope seems lost, you wait a sensible time before resending, and if your friend keeps saying 'still waiting for character 5,001' three times, you resend at once without waiting. That is TCP in a nutshell. In this lesson we see how TCP turns the principles of the last lesson into the real protocol behind the web, email and most apps.

What TCP is: TCP, the Transmission Control Protocol, first defined in RFC 793 in 1981 and updated many times since, is connection-oriented: before data flows, the two processes perform a handshake and set up state, such as sequence numbers and buffers. The connection exists only in the two end systems; routers in between know nothing about it. A TCP connection is full-duplex, so data can flow in both directions at once, and point-to-point, between exactly one sender and one receiver; TCP cannot multicast to many receivers.

The byte stream and buffers: When a client process writes data into its socket, TCP places it in the connection's send buffer. From time to time TCP grabs a chunk from the buffer, adds a header, and passes the segment to IP. At the other end, segments are placed in the receive buffer, and the application reads bytes from there. TCP does not see application messages; it sees a stream of bytes.

MSS and MTU: The maximum amount of application data in one segment is the maximum segment size, MSS. It is usually chosen so that a whole segment plus headers fits in the largest link-layer frame, the maximum transmission unit, MTU. Ethernet's MTU is 1,500 bytes. Subtract 20 bytes for the IP header and 20 bytes for the TCP header and you get the common MSS of 1,460 bytes. Note that MSS counts only data, not headers.

The segment structure: The TCP header is 20 bytes without options. Source port and destination port, 16 bits each, for multiplexing. Sequence number, 32 bits. Acknowledgement number, 32 bits. Header length, 4 bits, counting 32-bit words, so the value 5 means 20 bytes; it is needed because options make the header variable. Flag bits: ACK (the acknowledgement field is valid), SYN, FIN and RST (connection setup, teardown and reset), PSH (pass data up immediately), URG (urgent data), plus CWR and ECE used for congestion notification. Receive window, 16 bits, for flow control. Checksum, 16 bits, computed like UDP's. Urgent data pointer, 16 bits. Then options, such as MSS negotiation, window scaling, timestamps and selective acknowledgement.

Sequence numbers count bytes: TCP numbers bytes, not segments. The sequence number of a segment is the byte-stream number of the first byte in that segment. Example: a 500,000-byte file sent with MSS 1,000 bytes becomes 500 segments. If the first byte is numbered 0, the first segment has sequence number 0, the second 1,000, the third 2,000, and so on. In reality, each side picks a random initial sequence number, ISN, during the handshake, to reduce confusion with old segments from earlier connections and to make attacks harder; we used 0 just to keep the numbers simple.

Acknowledgement numbers mean 'next byte expected': The acknowledgement number that host A puts in a segment is the sequence number of the next byte A expects from B. If A has received bytes 0 to 535 from B, it puts 536 in the acknowledgement field. TCP acknowledgements are cumulative: an ACK of 536 says all bytes up to 535 arrived. If A has received bytes 0 to 535 and 900 to 1,000 but not 536 to 899, it still sends ACK 536.

Out-of-order segments: What does a TCP receiver do with segments that arrive out of order, like bytes 900 to 1,000 above? The standard leaves it to the implementation. In practice, receivers keep them in the buffer and wait for the gap to be filled, which saves bandwidth. This is closer to Selective Repeat than to Go-Back-N.

The Telnet example, worked: A client and server use an echo application where every typed character is sent and echoed back. Say the client's starting sequence number is 42 and the server's is 79. The user types C. Segment 1, client to server: Seq = 42, ACK = 79, data 'C'. Segment 2, server to client: Seq = 79, ACK = 43, data 'C' (the echo); ACK 43 says 'I got byte 42, send 43 next'. Segment 3, client to server: Seq = 43, ACK = 80, no data; it simply acknowledges the echo. Notice how the ACK for client data rides inside the server's data segment. This is called piggybacking.

Why TCP needs a good timeout: TCP uses a retransmission timer, like rdt3.0. The timeout must be longer than the round-trip time, or TCP retransmits needlessly; but if it is far longer, TCP reacts slowly to loss. The RTT on a real path changes all the time with queuing delays, so TCP must keep measuring and adapting.

Measuring RTT: SampleRTT is the time from sending a segment until its ACK arrives. TCP takes a sample for one segment at a time, roughly once per RTT, and never for retransmitted segments, because then it would not know whether the ACK belongs to the first or the second transmission. Since samples jump around, TCP keeps a smoothed average: EstimatedRTT = (1 - alpha) x EstimatedRTT + alpha x SampleRTT, with alpha = 0.125. This is an exponentially weighted moving average: recent samples count more, but one strange sample does not swing it wildly.

Measuring variability: TCP also tracks how much the RTT varies: DevRTT = (1 - beta) x DevRTT + beta x |SampleRTT - EstimatedRTT|, with beta = 0.25. Then the timeout is TimeoutInterval = EstimatedRTT + 4 x DevRTT. When samples are steady, DevRTT is small and the timeout stays close to the RTT. When samples fluctuate, the safety margin grows. The initial timeout before any sample is 1 second, and every time a timeout fires, TCP doubles the timeout interval for the next try, a simple form of backing off when the network seems troubled.

RTT worked example: Suppose EstimatedRTT = 100 ms and DevRTT = 10 ms, and a new SampleRTT of 120 ms arrives. Following RFC 6298, DevRTT is updated first using the old estimate: DevRTT = 0.75 x 10 + 0.25 x |120 - 100| = 7.5 + 5 = 12.5 ms. Then EstimatedRTT = 0.875 x 100 + 0.125 x 120 = 87.5 + 15 = 102.5 ms. TimeoutInterval = 102.5 + 4 x 12.5 = 152.5 ms. Some textbooks compute DevRTT with the new EstimatedRTT, which gives slightly different numbers; in exams, state which order you use.

TCP's sender in three events: A simplified TCP sender reacts to three events. Data received from the application: create a segment with the next sequence number, pass it to IP, and if the timer is not running, start it; there is only one retransmission timer, for the oldest unacknowledged segment. Timeout: retransmit the segment that caused the timeout, that is, the oldest unacknowledged one, and restart the timer. ACK received with value y: if y is greater than SendBase, the oldest unacknowledged byte, then everything below y is acknowledged; set SendBase = y, and restart the timer if there are still unacknowledged segments.

Three interesting scenarios: Lost ACK: A sends bytes 92 to 99, B's ACK 100 is lost; A times out and resends 92; B, already having it, discards the data and resends ACK 100. Premature timeout: A sends segments at 92 and 100; both ACKs (100 and 120) are delayed; A times out and resends only segment 92, then gets ACK 120 and knows both arrived, so it does not resend 100. Cumulative ACK saves the day: ACK 100 is lost but ACK 120 arrives before the timeout; A knows B has everything up to 119 and resends nothing.

Delayed ACKs: When the receiver gets an in-order segment and everything before it was already acknowledged, it may wait up to 500 ms for another segment before sending an ACK, so one ACK can cover two segments. If a second in-order segment arrives, it sends one cumulative ACK at once. If an out-of-order segment arrives, showing a gap, it immediately sends a duplicate ACK for the next expected byte. If a segment fills a gap, it ACKs immediately.

Fast retransmit: Waiting for a timeout can be slow. But the sender gets a hint earlier: duplicate ACKs. If a segment is lost and later segments arrive, the receiver keeps sending the same ACK number again. When the sender receives three duplicate ACKs for the same data, that is, four identical ACKs in total, it assumes the segment after that point was lost and retransmits it immediately, before its timer expires. Example: segments with Seq 100, 120, 140, 160, 180 are sent and segment 120 is lost. The receiver sends ACK 120 for segment 100, then ACK 120 again for 140, 160 and 180. On the third duplicate, the sender resends 120 at once.

Go-Back-N or Selective Repeat?: TCP is a mixture. Like GBN, it uses cumulative ACKs and a single timer, and the sender tracks only SendBase and the next sequence number. Like SR, receivers buffer out-of-order segments, and on timeout TCP resends only one segment, not the whole window. With the selective acknowledgement option, SACK, the receiver can report exactly which blocks arrived, making TCP even more like Selective Repeat.

Real life example 1, downloading a lecture PDF on Wi-Fi: A 5 MB PDF from a university portal travels as about 3,600 segments of 1,460 bytes. On a noisy hostel Wi-Fi, a few segments are lost. Each loss usually causes three duplicate ACKs within a few milliseconds, so fast retransmit repairs it long before a timeout would. The PDF still opens perfectly, because TCP reorders and fills every gap before handing bytes to the browser.

Real life example 2, a laggy remote login: A student uses SSH from home in Mymensingh to a lab server in Dhaka. Each keystroke travels in a tiny segment, and the echo and its ACK come back piggybacked, exactly as in the Telnet example. When the evening network is congested, RTT samples swing between 40 and 300 ms; DevRTT grows, so the timeout grows too, preventing a storm of needless retransmissions.

Common mistakes: Numbering segments instead of bytes. Writing the ACK as the last byte received instead of the next byte expected. Forgetting that MSS excludes headers. Measuring RTT on retransmitted segments. Counting three duplicate ACKs as three ACKs total instead of three duplicates after the original. Forgetting the factor 4 in TimeoutInterval.

What exams ask: Draw the TCP header with field sizes. Given an MSS and file size, list sequence numbers. Fill in Seq and ACK values in a Telnet-like exchange. Compute EstimatedRTT, DevRTT and TimeoutInterval for a sequence of samples. Trace scenarios with lost ACKs and premature timeouts. Explain fast retransmit with a worked example. Compare TCP with GBN and SR.

Recap: TCP is connection-oriented, full-duplex, point-to-point and byte-stream based. Its 20-byte header carries ports, 32-bit sequence and acknowledgement numbers, flags and a receive window. Sequence numbers count bytes, and ACKs are cumulative, naming the next byte expected. The timeout is EstimatedRTT plus 4 DevRTT, adapted from samples with weights 0.125 and 0.25. Three duplicate ACKs trigger fast retransmit. Next: how TCP opens and closes connections and avoids overflowing the receiver.
key_points: TCP is connection-oriented, full-duplex, point-to-point and treats data as a byte stream.
MSS is the maximum data per segment, typically 1,460 bytes for Ethernet's 1,500-byte MTU.
The TCP header is 20 bytes plus options: ports, 32-bit Seq and ACK, header length, flags, window, checksum, urgent pointer.
Sequence numbers count bytes; the ACK number is the next byte expected, and ACKs are cumulative.
EstimatedRTT = 0.875 EstimatedRTT + 0.125 SampleRTT; DevRTT uses beta = 0.25.
TimeoutInterval = EstimatedRTT + 4 DevRTT; the timeout doubles after each expiry.
RTT is not sampled for retransmitted segments.
Three duplicate ACKs trigger fast retransmit before the timer expires.
lessons.tip: For every Seq/ACK question, write a small table with columns: direction, Seq, ACK, data length. The next Seq is always the previous Seq plus data length, and the ACK is always the next byte expected. Mechanical rules beat guessing.
lessons.task: Start with EstimatedRTT = 80 ms and DevRTT = 8 ms. Apply SampleRTT values 100, 70 and 90 ms in turn and compute EstimatedRTT, DevRTT and TimeoutInterval after each one.

quiz.q: Host A has received bytes 0 to 999 from B. What acknowledgement number does A send?
quiz.explain: The ACK number is the next byte expected: 1000.

quiz.q: A 4,000-byte file is sent with MSS 1,000 and first sequence number 0. What is the third segment's sequence number?
quiz.explain: Segments start at 0, 1000, 2000, 3000; the third is 2000.

quiz.q: EstimatedRTT = 100 ms, DevRTT = 5 ms. What is TimeoutInterval?
When does TCP fast retransmit a segment?
quiz.explain: Three duplicate ACKs strongly suggest the next segment was lost.

quiz.q: With a 1,500-byte MTU and 20-byte IP and TCP headers, what is the MSS?

lessons.title: TCP Connection Management and Flow Control: Handshakes, Teardown and the Receive Window
lessons.content:
Think of a phone call. You dial; your friend picks up and says 'hello?'; you say 'hello, it's me'. Only then does the real talk begin. At the end, you say 'okay, bye'; she says 'bye'; both hang up. Nobody starts talking before the other picks up, and nobody cuts the line in the middle of a sentence. TCP does the same: a careful opening, a careful closing, and in between, it makes sure it never talks faster than the listener can write down. This lesson covers those three pieces: connection setup, connection teardown and flow control.

Why a handshake at all: Before data flows, both sides must agree that a connection exists and must learn each other's starting sequence numbers. They also exchange options such as MSS and window scaling, and allocate buffers and variables. Without this agreement, a receiver could not know which byte numbers to expect, and a stray old segment could be mistaken for new data. The handshake also proves that the client can actually receive at the address it claims, which matters for security.

Step 1, SYN: The client sends a special segment with no application data and the SYN flag set to 1. It picks a random initial sequence number, client_isn, and puts it in the sequence number field. This segment is sent inside an IP datagram to the server. Picking a random ISN makes it hard for an attacker to guess valid sequence numbers and reduces confusion with segments from old connections that used the same ports.

Step 2, SYNACK: When the SYN arrives, the server allocates buffers and variables for the connection and replies with a segment that also has no data. Its SYN flag is 1, its acknowledgement field is client_isn + 1, and its sequence number is the server's own random initial sequence number, server_isn. This segment says, in effect: 'I received your SYN starting at client_isn. I agree to the connection. My initial sequence number is server_isn.' It is called the SYNACK segment.

Step 3, ACK: On receiving the SYNACK, the client allocates its own buffers and variables and sends a final segment with SYN = 0, sequence number client_isn + 1 and acknowledgement server_isn + 1. This third segment may already carry application data, such as an HTTP request. After these three segments, the connection is established and both sides can send data. That is why it is called the three-way handshake, and why every new TCP connection costs one RTT before data can flow.

Worked handshake: Client ISN = 1000, server ISN = 5000. Segment 1, client to server: SYN, Seq = 1000. Segment 2, server to client: SYN + ACK, Seq = 5000, ACK = 1001. Segment 3, client to server: ACK, Seq = 1001, ACK = 5001, possibly with 200 bytes of HTTP request. If it carries 200 bytes, the server's next ACK will be 1201. Notice that the SYN consumes one sequence number even though it carries no data; so does the FIN.

Why three and not two: With only two messages, the server would set up a connection as soon as a SYN arrived. If an old, delayed SYN from a previous connection suddenly appeared, the server would open a half-connection that the client never wanted, and the client would not know the server's ISN for sure. The third message confirms that the client really is alive, wants this connection and has the server's ISN. Two generals trying to agree over an unreliable messenger can never be completely sure, but three messages is the practical compromise TCP uses.

Closing a connection: Either side can end the connection. Suppose the client decides to close. It sends a segment with the FIN flag set. The server replies with an ACK. The server then sends its own FIN when it has no more data to send, and the client acknowledges it. So closing typically takes four segments, though the server's ACK and FIN can be combined into one. Because the connection is full-duplex, each direction is closed separately; after the client's FIN, the server can still send data to the client until it sends its own FIN. This is called a half-close.

TIME_WAIT: After the client sends the final ACK, it does not disappear at once. It waits in the TIME_WAIT state for twice the maximum segment lifetime, commonly 30 seconds to 2 minutes depending on the system. Two reasons: if the final ACK is lost, the server will resend its FIN, and the client must still be around to ACK it again; and waiting ensures that any delayed segments of this connection die out in the network before the same port pair can be reused for a new connection. Busy servers that actively close many connections can accumulate thousands of sockets in TIME_WAIT, which is a known tuning issue.

The TCP states: A typical client goes through CLOSED, then SYN_SENT after sending SYN, ESTABLISHED after receiving SYNACK and sending ACK, FIN_WAIT_1 after sending FIN, FIN_WAIT_2 after receiving the ACK of its FIN, TIME_WAIT after receiving the server's FIN and sending ACK, then CLOSED again. A typical server goes through CLOSED, LISTEN after the application calls listen, SYN_RCVD after receiving SYN and sending SYNACK, ESTABLISHED after receiving the ACK, CLOSE_WAIT after receiving the client's FIN, LAST_ACK after sending its own FIN, and CLOSED after the final ACK. You can see these state names in the output of netstat.

Reset segments: What if a SYN arrives for a port where no process is listening? The host replies with a segment that has the RST flag set, meaning: 'there is no socket for that, do not resend.' This is what produces 'connection refused' on the client. For UDP, the equivalent is an ICMP port unreachable message. Port scanners like nmap use exactly these responses: a SYNACK means the port is open, an RST means closed, and silence often means a firewall is dropping packets.

SYN flood attack: In the handshake, the server allocates resources after just the first SYN. An attacker can send huge numbers of SYNs with fake source addresses and never complete the handshake. The server's table of half-open connections fills up, and real clients are refused. This denial-of-service attack is called a SYN flood. A clever defence is SYN cookies: the server does not store anything for a SYN. Instead it creates its ISN as a cryptographic hash of the source and destination addresses and ports plus a secret number. Only when a valid ACK comes back, with the acknowledgement number equal to that ISN plus one, does the server recompute the hash, verify it, and create the connection. Fake SYNs therefore cost almost nothing.

Flow control, the problem: TCP puts arriving bytes in a receive buffer, and the application reads from it when it is ready. If the application is slow, maybe busy with other work or running on a cheap phone, and the sender keeps sending fast, the buffer overflows and data is lost. Flow control is a speed-matching service: it keeps the sender from overflowing the receiver's buffer. Do not confuse it with congestion control, which keeps senders from overwhelming the network in between; both slow the sender down, but for different reasons.

The receive window: The receiver tells the sender how much free buffer space it has, in the 16-bit receive window field, rwnd, of every segment it sends back. Define RcvBuffer as the buffer size, LastByteRead as the last byte the application has read, and LastByteRcvd as the last byte that has arrived and been placed in the buffer. Then rwnd = RcvBuffer - (LastByteRcvd - LastByteRead). The sender makes sure that LastByteSent - LastByteAcked is at most rwnd, so the amount of unacknowledged data in flight never exceeds the free space.

Flow control worked: RcvBuffer = 65,536 bytes. The receiver has received up to byte 40,000 and the application has read up to byte 10,000. Data in the buffer = 40,000 - 10,000 = 30,000 bytes. rwnd = 65,536 - 30,000 = 35,536 bytes. If the sender has sent up to byte 60,000 and received ACKs up to 40,001, it has 20,000 bytes in flight, so it may send at most 35,536 - 20,000 = 15,536 more bytes until more ACKs or a larger rwnd arrive.

Zero window: If the application stops reading, rwnd eventually becomes 0, and the sender must stop. But how will the sender learn when space frees up, if the receiver has nothing to send? TCP handles this: while rwnd is 0, the sender keeps sending tiny probe segments with one data byte. The receiver acknowledges them, and each ACK carries the current rwnd, so as soon as the application reads and space opens, the sender finds out and resumes.

Window scaling: The rwnd field is 16 bits, so it can say at most 65,535 bytes. On fast long links, that is too small: with an RTT of 100 ms, 65,535 bytes per RTT is only about 5 Mbps. The window scale option, agreed during the handshake, multiplies the window value by a power of 2, allowing windows of up to about 1 GB. This is one reason SYN segments carry options.

Real life example 1, opening a website: Every time you open a new HTTPS site, your phone sends SYN, the server replies SYNACK, your phone sends ACK and immediately follows with the TLS handshake. On a 4G link with 60 ms RTT, the TCP handshake alone costs 60 ms before anything else happens. That is why browsers keep connections open and why HTTP/3 over QUIC tries to merge the transport and security handshakes.

Real life example 2, a slow phone receiving a large file: A friend sends you a large video over a local file-sharing app using TCP while your budget phone is also busy updating apps. Your phone's app reads from its socket slowly, the receive buffer fills, and rwnd shrinks, sometimes to zero. The sender pauses automatically, then speeds up as soon as your phone catches up. No data is lost, and neither phone needed any special code; TCP flow control did it.

Common mistakes: Forgetting that SYN and FIN each consume one sequence number. Writing the SYNACK's ACK as client_isn instead of client_isn + 1. Thinking the client closes instantly after the last ACK; it waits in TIME_WAIT. Confusing flow control (protect the receiver) with congestion control (protect the network). Computing rwnd with the total received bytes instead of the bytes still in the buffer.

What exams ask: Draw the three-way handshake with sequence and ACK numbers for given ISNs. Explain why three segments are needed. Draw the connection teardown and explain TIME_WAIT. List the client and server state sequences. Explain the SYN flood and SYN cookies. Compute rwnd and the amount the sender may still send. Distinguish flow control from congestion control.

Recap: TCP opens connections with SYN, SYNACK and ACK, exchanging random ISNs and options, at the cost of one RTT. It closes each direction with a FIN and an ACK, and the active closer waits in TIME_WAIT. RST rejects segments for closed ports. SYN cookies defeat SYN floods. Flow control uses the receive window, rwnd = RcvBuffer - (LastByteRcvd - LastByteRead), so the sender never overflows the receiver; zero-window probes and window scaling handle the edge cases. Next we tackle the harder problem of not overflowing the network itself: congestion control.
key_points: Three-way handshake: SYN (client_isn), SYNACK (server_isn, ACK client_isn + 1), ACK (ACK server_isn + 1).
Random ISNs prevent confusion with old segments and make attacks harder; SYN and FIN each use one sequence number.
Teardown: each side sends FIN and gets an ACK; the connection can be half-closed.
The active closer waits in TIME_WAIT for twice the maximum segment lifetime.
Client states: CLOSED, SYN_SENT, ESTABLISHED, FIN_WAIT_1, FIN_WAIT_2, TIME_WAIT; server: LISTEN, SYN_RCVD, ESTABLISHED, CLOSE_WAIT, LAST_ACK.
RST answers segments for ports with no socket; SYN cookies defend against SYN floods.
Flow control: rwnd = RcvBuffer - (LastByteRcvd - LastByteRead); sender keeps unACKed data at most rwnd.
Zero-window probes restart a stalled sender; the window scale option allows windows above 65,535 bytes.
lessons.tip: Memorise the handshake as a three-line table with columns flag, Seq and ACK, using ISNs 1000 and 5000. Every exam variant just changes the numbers; the plus-one pattern never changes.
lessons.task: Run 'netstat -an' (or 'netstat -an | find "TIME_WAIT"' on Windows) after closing a few browser tabs. Count connections in ESTABLISHED, TIME_WAIT and CLOSE_WAIT states and explain which side closed each one.

quiz.q: Client ISN is 300 and server ISN is 800. What is the acknowledgement number in the SYNACK?
quiz.explain: The SYNACK acknowledges the SYN: client_isn + 1 = 301.

quiz.q: Why does the actively closing side wait in TIME_WAIT?
options: To re-ACK a retransmitted FIN and let old segments die out
quiz.explain: The final ACK may be lost, and delayed segments must expire before port reuse.

quiz.q: RcvBuffer = 10,000, LastByteRcvd = 7,000, LastByteRead = 4,000. What is rwnd?
What do SYN cookies protect against?
quiz.explain: The server keeps no state for a SYN until a valid ACK proves the client is real.

quiz.q: Which statement about flow control is correct?
options: It prevents the sender from overflowing the receiver's buffer
quiz.explain: Flow control matches the sender's speed to the receiver's reading speed.

lessons.title: TCP Congestion Control: Slow Start, AIMD, Tahoe, Reno and Fairness
lessons.content:
Think of the Dhaka-Chattogram highway on the day before Eid. If every bus driver pushes onto the road as fast as possible, the toll plazas jam, buses crawl, and in the end fewer people reach home per hour than on a normal day. Now imagine a rule: each driver starts slowly, speeds up while the road is clear, and cuts speed sharply the moment he sees a jam. Traffic flows much better for everyone. TCP congestion control is exactly that rule for the Internet, and it is one of the main reasons the Internet did not collapse as it grew.

What congestion is: Congestion happens when too many sources send too much data too fast for the network to handle. Router buffers fill, queuing delays grow, and packets are dropped. Flow control, from the last lesson, protects the receiver. Congestion control protects the network in between. Both slow the sender, but for different reasons. In the late 1980s, the early Internet suffered congestion collapse, where throughput fell to a tiny fraction of capacity because hosts kept retransmitting into full routers. Van Jacobson's congestion control algorithms, added to TCP in 1988, fixed this.

Cost 1, delay: Consider two senders sharing a router with an output link of capacity R and an infinite buffer. As the total sending rate approaches R, the throughput of each sender approaches R/2, but queuing delay grows without limit, just like traffic intensity approaching 1 in lesson 2. So even without loss, pushing the network to full capacity makes delays huge.

Cost 2, wasted retransmissions: With finite buffers, packets are dropped and must be retransmitted. If a sender retransmits a packet that was only delayed, not lost, the router forwards two copies, wasting capacity on duplicates. So the goodput, the rate of useful new data delivered, falls below the link capacity, even while the link looks busy.

Cost 3, wasted upstream work: When a packet crosses three routers and is dropped at the fourth, the capacity used on the first three links was wasted. In a big network under heavy load, more and more packets are dropped late in their paths, and the total useful throughput can actually fall as offered load rises. That is congestion collapse. The lesson is clear: senders must back off when the network is congested.

Two approaches: In network-assisted congestion control, routers give explicit feedback to senders, for example by setting a bit in packets. In end-to-end congestion control, the network gives no explicit feedback, and end systems infer congestion from what they observe: packet loss and growing delay. Classic TCP uses the end-to-end approach, treating loss as the main signal of congestion. A newer mechanism, ECN, adds network assistance, which we will see at the end.

The congestion window: The TCP sender keeps a variable called the congestion window, cwnd. It limits how much unacknowledged data can be in flight: LastByteSent - LastByteAcked must be at most min(cwnd, rwnd). Ignoring rwnd, the sender can send about cwnd bytes per RTT, so its sending rate is roughly cwnd / RTT bytes per second. Example: cwnd = 10 MSS = 14,600 bytes and RTT = 100 ms gives about 146,000 bytes per second, which is about 1.17 Mbps. By changing cwnd, TCP changes its speed.

TCP's guiding principles: First, a lost segment, detected by timeout or three duplicate ACKs, implies congestion, so the rate should be decreased. Second, an acknowledged segment means the network is delivering, so the rate can be increased. Third, bandwidth probing: TCP keeps increasing its rate until loss occurs, then backs off, then starts probing again. TCP is self-clocking: ACKs arriving quickly make cwnd grow quickly; slow ACKs make it grow slowly.

Slow start: A new connection starts with cwnd = 1 MSS, a deliberately cautious value. For every ACK received, cwnd increases by 1 MSS. So after the first RTT, one ACK makes cwnd 2; after the second RTT, two ACKs make it 4; then 8, 16 and so on. Despite its name, slow start grows exponentially, doubling every RTT. With MSS = 1,460 bytes and RTT = 200 ms, the initial rate is only about 58 kbps, but within a few RTTs it reaches megabits. Modern systems often start with a larger initial window, such as 10 MSS, but the doubling idea is the same.

When slow start ends: Slow start stops in one of three ways. If a timeout occurs, TCP sets a variable called ssthresh, slow start threshold, to cwnd / 2, resets cwnd to 1 MSS and starts slow start again. When cwnd reaches ssthresh, TCP leaves slow start and enters congestion avoidance, because doubling near the last known danger point would be reckless. If three duplicate ACKs arrive, TCP performs fast retransmit and enters fast recovery.

Congestion avoidance: In this state, TCP increases cwnd by just 1 MSS per RTT, a linear increase. In practice it adds MSS x (MSS / cwnd) bytes for each ACK, so that after a full window of ACKs, cwnd has grown by one MSS. Example: if cwnd = 10 MSS, each ACK adds a tenth of an MSS. On a timeout, TCP behaves as in slow start: ssthresh = cwnd / 2 and cwnd = 1 MSS. On three duplicate ACKs, it halves: ssthresh = cwnd / 2, and enters fast recovery.

Fast recovery: Three duplicate ACKs mean that segments are still arriving at the receiver, so the network is congested but not jammed. Cutting all the way to 1 MSS would be too harsh. In TCP Reno, the sender sets ssthresh = cwnd / 2 and cwnd = ssthresh + 3 MSS (counting the three segments that left the network), retransmits the missing segment, and increases cwnd by 1 MSS for each further duplicate ACK. When a new ACK arrives for the missing data, it sets cwnd = ssthresh and returns to congestion avoidance. The older TCP Tahoe had no fast recovery: on any loss, timeout or triple duplicate ACK, it set cwnd to 1 MSS and restarted slow start.

A worked trace, Tahoe versus Reno: Let ssthresh = 8 MSS at the start. RTT 1: cwnd = 1. RTT 2: 2. RTT 3: 4. RTT 4: 8, which reaches ssthresh, so congestion avoidance begins. RTT 5: 9. RTT 6: 10. RTT 7: 11. RTT 8: 12. Now three duplicate ACKs arrive. Both versions set ssthresh = 12 / 2 = 6. Tahoe drops cwnd to 1 and does slow start again: 1, 2, 4, then 6 at ssthresh, then 7, 8, and so on. Reno drops to about 6 (after fast recovery) and continues linearly: 6, 7, 8, 9. Reno recovers much faster. If instead a timeout had happened, both would drop to 1.

AIMD and the sawtooth: Ignoring slow start and timeouts, Reno's behaviour in steady state is additive increase, multiplicative decrease: add 1 MSS per RTT, halve on loss. A graph of cwnd over time looks like a sawtooth: climbing slowly, falling sharply, climbing again. If loss happens when cwnd reaches W, cwnd swings between W/2 and W, so average throughput is about 0.75 x W / RTT. A well-known approximation links throughput to the loss rate L: average throughput is about 1.22 x MSS / (RTT x square root of L). It shows why very high-speed long links need extremely low loss rates to be filled by classic TCP.

Fairness: Suppose K TCP connections share a bottleneck link of rate R. A congestion control is fair if each gets about R/K. AIMD tends towards fairness. Picture two connections. When both increase additively, they move along a 45-degree line, gaining equally. When loss occurs, both halve, which shrinks the larger one more. Repeating this, their shares converge to equal. In practice, connections with shorter RTTs grab more, since their windows grow faster. And an application can cheat by opening many parallel TCP connections: a browser with 9 connections against another app with 1 gets about 90% of the link.

TCP CUBIC: On fast, long paths, adding 1 MSS per RTT is too slow to refill a huge window after a loss. TCP CUBIC, the default in Linux and widely used, remembers the window size at which loss last happened, W_max. After a loss it grows quickly when far below W_max, slowly and carefully when close to it, and then probes beyond it, following a cubic function of time since the last loss rather than counting ACKs. This gives higher throughput on high-bandwidth paths while staying fair to other CUBIC flows.

Delay-based ideas and ECN: Waiting for loss means queues are already full. Delay-based approaches watch the RTT instead: if the measured RTT rises well above the minimum RTT, queues are building, so slow down before loss. Google's BBR is a well-known modern algorithm that models the bottleneck bandwidth and minimum RTT. Explicit Congestion Notification, ECN, lets a congested router mark two bits in the IP header instead of dropping the packet. The receiver echoes the mark to the sender using the ECE flag in TCP; the sender halves its window as if a loss had happened and confirms with the CWR flag. Congestion is signalled with no lost packets.

Real life example 1, a big download in the evening: You start downloading a 2 GB game update at 9 pm. In the first second, slow start ramps up quickly. Then, as the ISP's international link gets busy, losses appear now and then; each time, cwnd is halved and slowly regrows, so your download speed wobbles in a sawtooth pattern. Meanwhile your brother's video call on the same Wi-Fi still works, because your TCP keeps backing off instead of grabbing everything.

Real life example 2, a university lab sharing one link: Fifty students in a Rajshahi lab all start downloading the same software at once over a 100 Mbps link. Thanks to AIMD, the link is shared roughly equally, about 2 Mbps each, rather than one machine taking 90 Mbps. If one student uses a download manager that opens 10 connections, that student gets a much bigger share, which is why some networks limit connections per user.

Common mistakes: Thinking slow start is linear; it is exponential. Confusing ssthresh with cwnd. Forgetting that a timeout resets cwnd to 1 MSS even in Reno. Saying congestion avoidance doubles cwnd. Confusing congestion control with flow control. Forgetting that the effective window is min(cwnd, rwnd).

What exams ask: Explain the three costs of congestion. Compare end-to-end and network-assisted control. Trace cwnd over time for given ssthresh and loss events, for both Tahoe and Reno, and identify slow start and congestion avoidance periods on a graph. Compute sending rate from cwnd and RTT. Explain AIMD fairness with the two-connection diagram. Short notes on CUBIC and ECN.

Recap: Congestion wastes capacity through queuing delay, unnecessary retransmissions and upstream work on dropped packets. TCP controls congestion end to end with a congestion window: slow start doubles cwnd each RTT up to ssthresh, congestion avoidance adds 1 MSS per RTT, triple duplicate ACKs halve it with fast recovery (Reno), and timeouts reset it to 1 MSS. AIMD makes a sawtooth and drives fair sharing. CUBIC, delay-based methods and ECN improve on the classic scheme. This ends the transport layer; next we go down to the network layer and look inside routers.
key_points: Congestion costs: huge queuing delay, wasted retransmissions and wasted upstream capacity, up to congestion collapse.
TCP uses end-to-end control: loss (timeout or 3 duplicate ACKs) signals congestion.
The sender keeps unACKed data at most min(cwnd, rwnd); rate is about cwnd / RTT.
Slow start: cwnd starts at 1 MSS and doubles every RTT until ssthresh.
Congestion avoidance: cwnd grows by 1 MSS per RTT.
On timeout: ssthresh = cwnd / 2, cwnd = 1 MSS; on 3 duplicate ACKs, Reno halves cwnd and uses fast recovery, Tahoe goes to 1 MSS.
AIMD produces a sawtooth with average throughput about 0.75 W / RTT and converges to fair sharing.
CUBIC grows the window as a cubic function of time; ECN marks packets instead of dropping them.
lessons.tip: For every cwnd trace question, make a table with columns RTT number, cwnd, ssthresh and state (SS, CA, FR). Fill it row by row, applying one rule per event. Most errors come from forgetting to update ssthresh before changing cwnd.
lessons.task: Starting with cwnd = 1 MSS and ssthresh = 16 MSS, trace cwnd for 20 RTTs for TCP Reno, assuming three duplicate ACKs at RTT 12 and a timeout at RTT 18. Then plot the values on graph paper and label slow start and congestion avoidance.

quiz.q: During slow start, how does cwnd grow?
quiz.explain: Each ACK adds 1 MSS, so the window doubles each RTT.

quiz.q: cwnd = 20 MSS when three duplicate ACKs arrive in TCP Reno. What is the new ssthresh?
quiz.explain: ssthresh is set to half of cwnd: 10 MSS.

quiz.q: What does TCP Tahoe do on three duplicate ACKs?
options: Sets cwnd to 1 MSS and restarts slow start
quiz.explain: Tahoe has no fast recovery; any loss sends cwnd to 1 MSS.

quiz.q: cwnd = 20 x 1,000 bytes and RTT = 100 ms. The sending rate is about:
quiz.explain: 20,000 bytes per 0.1 s = 200,000 bytes/s = 1.6 Mbps.

quiz.q: Why does AIMD tend to give fair sharing?
options: Halving on loss reduces the larger window more, so windows converge
All connections have the same RTT
quiz.explain: Equal additive increase plus multiplicative decrease pulls the shares toward equality.

lessons.title: The Network Layer and Inside a Router: Forwarding, Routing, Queues and Scheduling
lessons.content:
Imagine the Sayedabad bus terminal on a busy morning. Buses roll in from Barishal, Khulna and Chattogram. At each gate a staff member glances at the destination board on every bus and points it to the correct exit lane: that is a quick, local decision made thousands of times a day. Meanwhile, in an office upstairs, planners study traffic and decide which routes buses should take through the country and update the lane instructions. The gate staff are forwarding; the planners are routing. Every Internet router does both, and in this lesson we open the box.

What the network layer does: The transport layer, which we just finished, runs only in hosts. The network layer runs in every host and every router. On the sending side, it takes segments from the transport layer, wraps them in datagrams and sends them toward the first router. Each router on the path examines the datagram's header and moves it toward the destination. On the receiving side, it extracts the segments and hands them to the transport layer. Routers do not run application or transport protocols for forwarding; their job is to move datagrams from input links to output links.

Forwarding: When a datagram arrives on an input link, the router must move it to the appropriate output link. This is forwarding, a router-local action, done in hardware in a few nanoseconds per packet. It uses a forwarding table: the router reads a header field, usually the destination IP address, looks it up in the table, and the table entry says which output port to use. Forwarding is the data plane of the network.

Routing: Routing is the network-wide process of determining the end-to-end paths that datagrams take from source to destination, and therefore of computing the forwarding tables. Routing algorithms take seconds, not nanoseconds, and are usually implemented in software. Routing is the control plane. The analogy: forwarding is like the driver deciding at each roundabout which exit to take according to a sign; routing is the planning of the whole trip from Dhaka to Sylhet.

The traditional control plane: In the classic Internet, every router runs a routing algorithm itself, as software on its own routing processor. Routers exchange routing messages with each other, such as link-state advertisements or distance vectors, and each one computes its own forwarding table. Control is distributed: there is no central brain. OSPF and BGP, which we will study later, work this way.

Software-defined networking: In the SDN approach, a logically centralised remote controller computes the forwarding tables and installs them in the routers, which become simpler packet switches. The controller sees the whole network, so it can apply global policies, for example sending video traffic on one path and backups on another, or quickly blocking an attacker. Big data centers and some large operators use SDN. The devices can also match on more than the destination address, such as ports or protocol, and take actions like forward, drop or modify, a generalisation called match plus action.

The service model: What does the Internet's network layer promise? Nothing beyond best effort. It does not guarantee delivery, timing, order or a minimum bandwidth. Other designs have offered more, for example ATM networks provided constant bit rate service with guaranteed delay. Yet best effort, combined with smart transport protocols, well-provisioned links and CDNs, turned out to be good enough for almost everything, including video calls. Simplicity won.

Inside a router, the big picture: A router has four main parts. Input ports, where packets arrive. A switching fabric, which connects input ports to output ports. Output ports, where packets leave. And a routing processor, which runs routing protocols, maintains routing tables and, in traditional routers, computes the forwarding table. In an SDN router, the routing processor instead talks to the remote controller.

Input ports: An input port does three things. First, physical layer line termination: receiving the bits from the cable or fiber. Second, link-layer processing: decapsulating the frame, for example removing the Ethernet header. Third, and most important, lookup: using the forwarding table to find the output port for this datagram. A copy of the forwarding table is kept in each input port so lookups happen locally, at line speed, without asking the routing processor. On a 10 Gbps link, a router may need to perform tens of millions of lookups per second. If packets arrive faster than the fabric can take them, they queue at the input port.

Destination-based lookup: For IPv4, the forwarding table maps ranges of destination addresses to output ports. The router uses longest prefix matching: if several entries match an address, the entry with the longest matching prefix wins. We will work through examples in the addressing lesson. Doing this fast needs special hardware, such as ternary content addressable memory, TCAM, which can compare an address against all entries in one clock cycle.

Switching fabric, three designs: Switching via memory: the earliest routers were ordinary computers; the input port copied each packet into memory, the CPU found the output, and copied it out. Each packet crosses memory twice, so if memory can handle B packets per second, throughput is less than B/2. Switching via a bus: the input port sends the packet over a shared bus to all output ports, and only the right one keeps it; only one packet can cross at a time, so the bus speed limits the router. Switching via an interconnection network: a crossbar connects N inputs to N outputs with 2N buses; several packets can cross at the same time as long as they go to different outputs. Modern high-end routers use such networks, often in several stages.

Output ports: An output port takes packets from the switching fabric, stores them in its queue, and transmits them on the outgoing link, performing the link-layer encapsulation and physical-layer transmission. Queuing here is very common: if packets from several inputs head to the same output at the same time, they must wait their turn.

Where queues form, a worked example: Suppose a router has N inputs and N outputs, each at R bps, and the fabric is N times faster than one line. If, in a burst, packets from all N inputs head for the same output, N packets arrive at that output in the time it can send only one. The queue grows by N - 1 packets in that interval. If bursts continue, the buffer fills and packets are dropped. This is exactly where most packet loss in the Internet happens: at router output queues.

Input queuing and head-of-line blocking: If the fabric is not fast enough, packets wait at the input ports. Then a problem appears: a packet at the front of an input queue waiting for a busy output blocks the packets behind it, even if their outputs are free. This is head-of-line blocking at the router level. Studies show that with HOL blocking and random traffic, input queues can grow without limit once the arrival rate reaches only about 58% of capacity. That is why routers use faster fabrics and virtual output queues, separate queues per output, at each input.

How much buffer: A long-standing rule of thumb says a router's buffer should be about RTT x C, where C is the link capacity and RTT a typical round-trip time, for example 250 ms. For a 10 Gbps link this gives 2.5 Gbit of buffer. Later research showed that with N large independent TCP flows, RTT x C divided by the square root of N is enough. Too much buffer is also harmful: queues stay full, delays grow, and interactive apps suffer, a problem nicknamed bufferbloat, often seen in home routers.

Dropping and marking: When the queue is full, the simplest policy is drop-tail: drop the arriving packet. Active queue management, AQM, instead drops or marks packets early, before the buffer is full, to signal TCP senders to slow down in time. Random Early Detection, RED, drops packets with a probability that grows with the average queue length. With ECN, the router marks instead of dropping, as we saw in congestion control.

Packet scheduling: Which queued packet goes next? First-in-first-out, FIFO, sends packets in arrival order, simple and common. Priority scheduling puts packets into classes, for example voice above email, and always sends from the highest non-empty class; low classes may starve. Round robin cycles among classes, sending one packet from each in turn. Weighted fair queuing, WFQ, gives each class i a weight w_i, and class i receives at least the fraction w_i / sum of all weights of the link rate when it has packets. Example: on a 10 Mbps link with two classes of weights 3 and 1, the first is guaranteed 7.5 Mbps and the second 2.5 Mbps.

Real life example 1, an ISP router at night: At 10 pm, traffic from thousands of homes in Uttara converges on the ISP's border router heading to international links. The output port toward the upstream provider queues packets; when it is full, drop-tail or AQM kicks in, and the TCP senders of all those Netflix and YouTube streams reduce their windows. What you experience as buffering at home is often happening right there, at one router output queue.

Real life example 2, an office router with priority: A software company in Dhaka runs video meetings with clients abroad while staff also download large files. The network admin configures priority queuing on the office router: voice and video packets go in a high-priority class, file downloads in a low one. Meetings stay smooth even when someone starts a 10 GB download, because the router always sends the meeting packets first.

Common mistakes: Confusing forwarding (local, per packet, nanoseconds) with routing (network-wide, seconds). Thinking routers need the transport header for forwarding. Thinking packets are mostly lost on links; most loss happens in router queues. Thinking bigger buffers always help. Mixing up HOL blocking in routers with HOL blocking in HTTP/1.1; the idea is the same but the place differs.

What exams ask: Distinguish forwarding and routing, and data plane and control plane. Compare the traditional per-router control plane with SDN. Draw a router's architecture and explain each part. Compare switching via memory, bus and interconnection network. Explain input and output queuing and HOL blocking. Compute buffer size by the RTT x C rule. Compare FIFO, priority, round robin and WFQ, and compute WFQ shares.

Recap: The network layer runs in every host and router. Forwarding moves packets from input to output using a forwarding table (data plane); routing computes those tables (control plane), either per router or via an SDN controller. The Internet offers only best-effort service. A router has input ports with local lookup, a switching fabric (memory, bus or crossbar), output ports with queues, and a routing processor. Queues cause delay and loss, and schedulers decide who goes next. Next we open the IPv4 datagram itself.
key_points: The network layer runs in every host and router; routers forward datagrams between links.
Forwarding is local, per packet, in hardware (data plane); routing computes paths and tables network-wide (control plane).
Traditional routers each run routing algorithms; in SDN a logically central controller installs tables.
The Internet's network layer offers only best-effort service: no guarantees of delivery, order, delay or bandwidth.
A router has input ports (lookup with a local table copy), a switching fabric, output ports and a routing processor.
Fabrics switch via memory (under B/2), via a shared bus, or via an interconnection network such as a crossbar.
Queues form at outputs and inputs; HOL blocking stalls input queues; buffer rule of thumb is RTT x C.
Schedulers: FIFO, priority, round robin, and WFQ with share w_i / sum of weights.
lessons.tip: Learn the router diagram as four boxes in a row: input port (three small boxes), fabric, output port (three small boxes), with the routing processor on top. Being able to draw it in one minute covers many short questions.
lessons.task: Run traceroute (tracert on Windows) to a site abroad at a quiet time and again at a busy evening hour. Compare the times at each hop and guess at which router output queues the extra delay builds up.

quiz.q: Which is a data plane function?
options: Moving a datagram from an input port to an output port
quiz.explain: Forwarding packets is the data plane; computing paths is the control plane.

quiz.q: If a memory-switched router's memory can handle B packets per second, its forwarding throughput is:
quiz.explain: Each packet is written to and read from memory, crossing it twice.

quiz.q: What is head-of-line blocking in a router?
options: A packet blocked by a firewall
Losing the first packet of a flow
A packet waiting for a busy output blocks packets behind it in the same input queue
quiz.explain: The front packet holds the queue even if later packets could go to free outputs.

quiz.q: Two WFQ classes have weights 4 and 1 on a 10 Mbps link. What is the first class guaranteed?
By the RTT x C rule, how much buffer for a 1 Gbps link with RTT 200 ms?
quiz.explain: 0.2 s x 1 Gbps = 0.2 Gbit = 200 Mbit.

lessons.title: The IPv4 Datagram: Header Fields, TTL, Checksum and Fragmentation
lessons.content:
Think of the address label on a courier parcel. It is not just a name and a house number. It has the sender's address, the receiver's address, a tracking number, the weight, whether the parcel is fragile, how many days it may stay in transit, and which department handles it. A sorting hub never opens the box; it reads only the label. An IPv4 header is that label for every packet on the Internet, and in this lesson we read it field by field and learn what happens when a parcel is too big for the next truck.

What IPv4 is: IP version 4, defined in RFC 791 in 1981, is the network-layer protocol that carries almost all Internet traffic, together with its successor IPv6. It provides best-effort, connectionless delivery of datagrams from one host to another, using 32-bit addresses. Every router on the path reads the header, decides where to forward, updates a few fields and sends it on. The design is deliberately simple so that routers can be fast.

The header at a glance: The IPv4 header is 20 bytes without options, laid out in rows of 32 bits. Row 1: version, header length, type of service, total length. Row 2: identification, flags, fragment offset. Row 3: time-to-live, upper-layer protocol, header checksum. Row 4: source IP address. Row 5: destination IP address. Then optional options, then the data, which is usually a TCP or UDP segment. Drawing these five rows is one of the most common exam questions in networking.

Version and header length: The version field, 4 bits, says which IP version this is: 4 for IPv4. Routers need it to interpret the rest correctly. The header length field, 4 bits, gives the header size in 32-bit words, because options can make the header longer. Most datagrams have no options, so the value is 5, meaning 5 x 4 = 20 bytes. The maximum value 15 means 60 bytes. Example: if the header length field is 6, the header is 24 bytes, so there are 4 bytes of options.

Type of service: This 8-bit field was meant to let datagrams be marked for special treatment, such as low delay or high throughput. Today its first 6 bits are the Differentiated Services Code Point, DSCP, used by networks to place packets into service classes, for example giving voice traffic priority. The last 2 bits are used for Explicit Congestion Notification, ECN, which we met in congestion control: a router can mark them instead of dropping a packet.

Total length: 16 bits giving the length of the whole datagram, header plus data, in bytes. The theoretical maximum is 2^16 - 1 = 65,535 bytes, but datagrams are rarely larger than 1,500 bytes, the Ethernet MTU. Example: a TCP segment with 1,460 bytes of data and a 20-byte TCP header inside an IPv4 datagram with a 20-byte header gives a total length of 1,500.

Time-to-live: TTL, 8 bits, prevents datagrams from circulating forever if routing goes wrong and creates a loop. The sender sets an initial value, commonly 64 or 128 depending on the operating system. Every router decreases it by one; if it reaches zero, the router discards the datagram and usually sends an ICMP time exceeded message back to the source. That is exactly what traceroute uses. If you receive a reply with TTL 117 from a server that probably started at 128, it crossed about 11 routers.

Protocol: 8 bits telling the destination which transport-layer protocol should receive the data: 6 for TCP, 17 for UDP, 1 for ICMP. This is the glue between the network and transport layers, just as the port number is the glue between transport and application. It is used only at the final destination.

Header checksum: 16 bits that help a router detect bit errors in the header, not the data. It is computed with the same one's complement method as the UDP checksum, treating the header as 16-bit words. If a router finds an error, it discards the datagram. Because TTL changes at every hop, every router must recompute the checksum and store the new value. Why have both an IP checksum and a TCP/UDP checksum? The IP one covers only the IP header; transport checksums cover the segment; and in principle IP could carry protocols other than TCP and UDP. IPv6 dropped the header checksum to speed up routers.

Source and destination addresses: 32 bits each. The sender puts its own IP address in the source field and the destination's IP address, usually obtained from DNS, in the destination field. Routers forward based on the destination address. The source address lets the receiver reply. Both normally stay the same from end to end, unless a NAT device rewrites them, as we will see later.

Options: Options allow the header to be extended for special uses such as recording the route or timestamps. They were rarely used, made header processing slower and variable in time, and some routers drop packets with options. IPv6 removed options from the main header and replaced them with optional extension headers.

Overhead in practice: A typical TCP/IP datagram carries 40 bytes of headers: 20 for IP, 20 for TCP, plus the application message. For a short message such as a chat 'ok' of 2 bytes, 40 bytes of headers is 95% overhead. For a 1,460-byte data segment, 40 bytes is under 3%. This is why protocols batch data when they can and why header compression exists on slow links like some cellular connections.

Why fragmentation: Each link layer has a maximum frame payload, the MTU. Ethernet's MTU is 1,500 bytes. Some links have smaller MTUs. Paths may cross different link types. When a router receives a datagram that is too large for the next link's MTU, IPv4 allows it to split the datagram into smaller pieces called fragments, each a full IP datagram with its own header. The fragments travel independently and are reassembled only at the destination host, never by routers along the way, which keeps routers simple.

The fields that make it work: Identification, 16 bits, is a number the sender assigns to each datagram; all fragments of one datagram carry the same identification, so the receiver knows they belong together. Flags, 3 bits: one is reserved, DF means do not fragment, and MF means more fragments follow. The last fragment has MF = 0; all others have MF = 1. Fragment offset, 13 bits, tells where this fragment's data belongs in the original datagram, measured in units of 8 bytes. Because of the 8-byte unit, every fragment except the last must carry a multiple of 8 bytes of data.

Worked fragmentation example: A 4,000-byte datagram (20 bytes of header plus 3,980 bytes of data) with identification 777 arrives at a router whose outgoing link has an MTU of 1,500 bytes. Each fragment can carry at most 1,500 - 20 = 1,480 bytes of data, and 1,480 is a multiple of 8. Fragment 1: data bytes 0 to 1,479, total length 1,500, offset 0, MF = 1. Fragment 2: data bytes 1,480 to 2,959, total length 1,500, offset 1,480 / 8 = 185, MF = 1. Fragment 3: data bytes 2,960 to 3,979, that is 1,020 bytes, total length 1,040, offset 2,960 / 8 = 370, MF = 0. Check: 1,480 + 1,480 + 1,020 = 3,980. All three carry identification 777.

A second example, when the MTU is awkward: A 2,000-byte datagram (1,980 bytes of data) must cross a link with MTU 1,006 bytes. The room for data is 1,006 - 20 = 986 bytes, but 986 is not a multiple of 8, so each non-final fragment can carry only 984 bytes (123 x 8). Fragment 1: 984 data bytes, total length 1,004, offset 0, MF = 1. Fragment 2: 984 bytes, total length 1,004, offset 984 / 8 = 123, MF = 1. Fragment 3: the remaining 1,980 - 1,968 = 12 bytes, total length 32, offset 1,968 / 8 = 246, MF = 0. Forgetting to round down to a multiple of 8 is the most common mistake in these questions.

Reassembly at the destination: The receiving host collects fragments with the same source, destination, protocol and identification. It places each fragment's data at position offset x 8. When it has the fragment with MF = 0 and no gaps remain, the datagram is complete and goes up to the transport layer. If any fragment is lost, the whole datagram is lost; IP does not retransmit fragments, and the receiver discards the partial data after a timeout. TCP then retransmits the whole segment. So fragmentation turns one loss into the loss of a much larger unit, one reason it is avoided.

Avoiding fragmentation: Path MTU discovery lets a sender learn the smallest MTU on the path. The sender sets the DF flag. If a router cannot forward because the datagram is too big, it drops it and sends back an ICMP message saying fragmentation is needed, including the next link's MTU. The sender then lowers its packet size. TCP also negotiates MSS during the handshake to stay below the MTU. IPv6 goes further: routers never fragment; only the source can, using an extension header.

Real life example 1, a VPN on home broadband: Some home users in Bangladesh connect to an office VPN, which wraps each packet inside another header. A 1,500-byte packet plus VPN headers becomes larger than 1,500 bytes. If path MTU discovery is blocked by a firewall that drops ICMP, large packets silently disappear while small ones work: websites half-load, emails with attachments hang. The common fix is to lower the MTU or clamp the TCP MSS on the router, a direct application of this lesson.

Real life example 2, reading TTL from ping: You ping a server and see TTL = 54 in the replies. Linux servers usually start at 64, so the reply crossed about 10 routers. Pinging a device on your own Wi-Fi shows TTL 64 or 128 unchanged, since no router was crossed. Network engineers use this quick trick to guess distance and even the operating system of a remote host.

Common mistakes: Forgetting that header length is counted in 4-byte words and offset in 8-byte units. Using 1,500 instead of 1,480 as the data per fragment. Setting MF = 1 on the last fragment. Thinking routers reassemble fragments. Thinking the IP checksum covers the data. Forgetting that TTL changes, so the checksum must be recomputed at every hop.

What exams ask: Draw the IPv4 header with field sizes and explain each field. Compute the header length from the field value. Fragment a given datagram for a given MTU, listing total length, offset and MF for each fragment. Explain why reassembly happens only at the destination. Explain TTL and how traceroute uses it. Compare the IPv4 checksum with the TCP checksum.

Recap: The IPv4 header is 20 bytes plus options: version, header length, DSCP/ECN, total length, identification, flags, fragment offset, TTL, protocol, header checksum, and source and destination addresses. TTL stops loops; protocol says TCP (6), UDP (17) or ICMP (1); the checksum covers only the header and is recomputed at each hop. Datagrams larger than the next link's MTU are fragmented using identification, MF and offset in 8-byte units, and reassembled only at the destination. Next we study the addresses themselves: IPv4 addressing and subnetting.
key_points: The IPv4 header is 20 bytes without options, in five 32-bit rows.
Header length counts 32-bit words (5 means 20 bytes); total length counts header plus data, maximum 65,535.
The type of service byte now carries DSCP (6 bits) and ECN (2 bits).
TTL is decreased at every router; at 0 the datagram is dropped and ICMP time exceeded is sent.
Protocol field: 6 = TCP, 17 = UDP, 1 = ICMP.
The header checksum covers only the header and is recomputed at each hop because TTL changes.
Fragmentation uses identification, the MF and DF flags, and a 13-bit offset in units of 8 bytes.
Worked: a 4,000-byte datagram on a 1,500 MTU becomes fragments of 1,480, 1,480 and 1,020 data bytes with offsets 0, 185, 370.
lessons.tip: For fragmentation, always compute the data per fragment first as (MTU - 20), round down to a multiple of 8, and then write a three-column table: data bytes, offset (start / 8) and MF. The total length column is just data plus 20.
lessons.task: Fragment a 5,000-byte IPv4 datagram (20-byte header) for a link with MTU 1,000 bytes. List each fragment's total length, offset and MF flag, and check that the data adds up to 4,980 bytes.

quiz.q: The header length field is 5. How long is the header?
quiz.explain: The field counts 32-bit words: 5 x 4 = 20 bytes.

quiz.q: A fragment starts at data byte 2,960 of the original datagram. What is its offset field value?
quiz.explain: Offset is in 8-byte units: 2,960 / 8 = 370.

quiz.q: Why must every router recompute the IPv4 header checksum?
options: The TTL field changes at each hop
quiz.explain: Decrementing TTL changes the header, so the checksum must be updated.

quiz.q: Where are IPv4 fragments reassembled?
quiz.explain: Reassembly happens only at the destination, keeping routers simple.

quiz.q: Which protocol number means the datagram carries TCP?
quiz.explain: 6 is TCP, 17 is UDP, 1 is ICMP.

lessons.title: IPv4 Addressing and Subnetting: CIDR, Masks, Host Counts and Longest Prefix Match
lessons.content:
Think of a postal address in Dhaka: Dhaka 1207, Road 5, House 12, Flat 3B. The first part, the area code, tells the national post where to send the letter. Inside that area, the road narrows it down, and inside the road, the house and flat. Nobody in Chattogram needs to know every flat in Mohammadpur; they only need to know that 1207 means Dhaka. IPv4 addresses work the same way: the first bits name a network, the remaining bits name a host inside it. Getting comfortable with this split, and with the binary arithmetic behind it, is one of the most practical skills in this course.

What an IP address names: An IP address belongs to an interface, the boundary between a host or router and a physical link, not to a whole machine. A laptop with Wi-Fi and Ethernet has two interfaces and can have two addresses. A router connects several links, so it has several interfaces, each with its own address. Every IPv4 address is 32 bits long, so there are 2^32, about 4.3 billion, possible addresses.

Dotted-decimal notation: The 32 bits are written as four bytes in decimal, separated by dots. Example: 193.32.216.9 is 11000001 00100000 11011000 00001001 in binary. Converting: 193 = 128 + 64 + 1, so 11000001. 32 is 00100000. 216 = 128 + 64 + 16 + 8, so 11011000. 9 is 00001001. Each byte ranges from 0 to 255. Being able to convert any byte quickly using the place values 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 is the foundation of everything that follows.

What a subnet is: Interfaces that can reach each other directly, without passing through a router, form a subnet. In a typical home, the laptop, phones and the router's LAN interface are one subnet. They share the same leftmost bits of their addresses, for example all starting with 192.168.1. To find subnets in a network diagram, imagine detaching each interface from its router; each island of connected interfaces that remains is a subnet. Even a point-to-point link between two routers is its own small subnet.

The old classful system: Originally, addresses were split into classes by their first bits. Class A started with 0, used 8 network bits, so first bytes 1 to 126, with about 16 million hosts per network. Class B started with 10, 16 network bits, first bytes 128 to 191, about 65,000 hosts. Class C started with 110, 24 network bits, first bytes 192 to 223, only 254 hosts. Class D, 224 to 239, is for multicast; class E, 240 to 255, was reserved. The 127 block is for loopback, such as 127.0.0.1. The problem: a company needing 2,000 addresses got a whole class B with 65,534 hosts, wasting most of them, and class B blocks ran out fast.

CIDR, the modern way: Classless Interdomain Routing, CIDR, allows the network part to be any length. An address is written a.b.c.d/x, where x is the number of leading bits in the network part, called the prefix. The remaining 32 - x bits identify hosts. Example: 200.23.16.0/23 means the first 23 bits are the network, and 9 bits are for hosts, giving 2^9 = 512 addresses. An organisation now gets a block sized close to its needs, not a fixed class.

The subnet mask: The prefix length can also be written as a mask: x ones followed by 32 - x zeros. /24 is 255.255.255.0. /26 is 255.255.255.192, because the last byte is 11000000 = 192. /20 is 255.255.240.0, because the third byte is 11110000 = 240. Useful last-byte values to memorise: 128, 192, 224, 240, 248, 252, 254, 255 for 1 to 8 ones. To find the network address, perform a bitwise AND of the IP address and the mask.

Host counts: If there are h host bits, there are 2^h addresses in the block. Two are special: the all-zeros host part is the network address itself, and the all-ones host part is the broadcast address for that subnet. So the number of usable host addresses is 2^h - 2. A /24 has 2^8 - 2 = 254 hosts; a /26 has 2^6 - 2 = 62; a /30, often used for point-to-point router links, has 2^2 - 2 = 2, exactly enough for the two routers.

Worked example 1: Find the network, broadcast and host range of 192.168.10.77/26. The mask is 255.255.255.192, and the block size in the last byte is 256 - 192 = 64. Blocks start at 0, 64, 128, 192. Since 77 is between 64 and 127, the network address is 192.168.10.64 and the broadcast address is 192.168.10.127. Usable hosts are 192.168.10.65 to 192.168.10.126, which is 62 hosts. Check in binary: 77 = 01001101; AND with 11000000 gives 01000000 = 64.

Worked example 2, a different byte: Find the network of 172.16.45.200/20. A /20 mask is 255.255.240.0, so the interesting byte is the third one, with block size 256 - 240 = 16. Blocks in the third byte start at 0, 16, 32, 48. Since 45 is between 32 and 47, the network is 172.16.32.0 and the broadcast is 172.16.47.255. There are 2^12 - 2 = 4,094 usable hosts.

Subnetting a block, worked: A college gets 200.10.20.0/24 and wants 4 equal subnets for 4 departments. 4 subnets need 2 extra bits, since 2^2 = 4, so the new prefix is /26. The subnets are 200.10.20.0/26, 200.10.20.64/26, 200.10.20.128/26 and 200.10.20.192/26, each with 62 usable hosts. If it wanted 8 subnets, it would borrow 3 bits, use /27, with block size 32 and 30 hosts each.

VLSM, different sizes for different needs: Real departments are not equal. Suppose, from 200.10.20.0/24, CSE needs 100 hosts, EEE needs 50 and the office needs 20. Allocate the largest first. 100 hosts need 7 host bits (126 usable), so /25: 200.10.20.0/25 (hosts .1 to .126). 50 hosts need 6 bits (62), so /26: 200.10.20.128/26 (.129 to .190). 20 hosts need 5 bits (30), so /27: 200.10.20.192/27 (.193 to .222). Left over: 200.10.20.224/27 for future use. This is variable-length subnet masking, VLSM, and it wastes far fewer addresses than equal subnets.

Route aggregation: CIDR also lets ISPs advertise one big prefix instead of many small ones.
